title: Electron-Induced Formation of C$_{2}$ on Si(100) from Acetylene and Ethylene
comment: Manuscript is pages 1-25, 8 Figures. Supplementary Information is pages 24-35, with 15 Figures
summary: Hydrogen Desorption Lithography on Si(100) demonstrates the ability of the Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) to create functional atomic-scale structures and devices. The dehydrogenation of adsorbed molecules represents a potential complementary technique that has received little attention. For example, formation of C$_{2}$ could introduce local strain or act as centers for subsequent reactions and would inform positionally controlled mechanosynthesis, an approach with vast potential in surface patterning and functionalization. Here, we studied the electron-induced dehydrogenation of acetylene and ethylene on Si(100) at 4 K using STM. Excitation of acetylene at +3.2 V and above induces configurational switching, including to a new sublayer-bonded geometry previously predicted to be an adsorption precursor, as well as migration and desorption. Excitation also induces dehydrogenation to C$_{2}$. Switching between three observed C$_{2}$ configurations can be induced by excitation at +4.2 V and above. Simulations using density functional theory reproduced the experimental images based on choice of functional, dimer-buckling averaging, and inclusion of diffuse basis functions. In addition, dehydrogenation could be induced using field-emitted electrons on a scale ranging from a single molecule to a radius of >10 nm. These observations highlight the potential of carbon dehydrogenation as an additional tool in Atomically Precise Fabrication (APF).

AI.tldr: This paper investigates electron-induced dehydrogenation of acetylene and ethylene on Si(100) using STM at 4 K, demonstrating controlled dehydrogenation to C₂ configurations and highlighting its potential for atomically precise fabrication.
AI.motivation: Dehydrogenation of adsorbed molecules on Si(100) is a complementary technique to hydrogen desorption lithography that has received little attention, yet could enable local strain introduction, reaction centers, and positionally controlled mechanosynthesis for surface patterning and functionalization.
AI.method: STM-based electron-induced excitation at cryogenic temperatures (4 K) on acetylene and ethylene adsorbed on Si(100), combined with density functional theory simulations to reproduce experimental images and validate observed configurations.
AI.result: Excitation of acetylene at ≥+3.2 V induces configurational switching, including a sublayer-bonded adsorption precursor, migration, desorption, and dehydrogenation to C₂. Three C₂ configurations were observed and switchable at ≥+4.2 V. Dehydrogenation was achievable from single-molecule to >10 nm radius using field-emitted electrons.
AI.conclusion: Carbon dehydrogenation is a viable additional tool in atomically precise fabrication, enabling controlled creation of C₂ structures with potential applications in mechanosynthesis and nanoscale surface patterning.

title: Photoemission from Semi-Infinite Crystals: An \emph{Ab Initio} Scattering-State Approach
summary: Photoemission is an escape problem, yet first-principles calculations usually trap the electron in a periodic box. We present a parameter-free \emph{ab initio} framework that removes this artificial boundary by constructing open scattering states for semi-infinite crystal-vacuum interfaces from Wannier Hamiltonians and Green-function embedding. The method gives continuum-normalized time-reversed LEED final states with microscopic quasiparticle attenuation. For Ag(111), it predicts absolute quantum efficiency, vectorial photoemission, and mean transverse energy on the experimental scale.

AI.tldr: A parameter-free ab initio framework using Wannier Hamiltonians and Green-function embedding constructs open scattering states for photoemission, enabling accurate predictions of quantum efficiency, vectorial photoemission, and mean transverse energy for Ag(111).
AI.motivation: Photoemission is inherently an escape problem, but standard first-principles calculations trap electrons in a periodic box, introducing artificial boundaries that fail to capture the true semi-infinite nature of crystal-vacuum interfaces.
AI.method: The method constructs continuum-normalized time-reversed LEED final states by building open scattering states for semi-infinite crystal-vacuum interfaces using Wannier Hamiltonians and Green-function embedding, incorporating microscopic quasiparticle attenuation.
AI.result: For Ag(111), the method predicts absolute quantum efficiency, vectorial photoemission, and mean transverse energy that match experimental scales.
AI.conclusion: Removing the artificial periodic boundary through open scattering states enables parameter-free ab initio predictions of photoemission observables directly comparable to experiment.

title: Assessing the Influence of d-Orbital Radius on the Formation of Localized Photogenerated States in Corundum Metal Oxides
summary: Photogenerated polarons are fundamental to the photophysics of transition metal oxide semiconductors. It is therefore imperative to understand the mechanisms by which polarons form upon photoexcitation of transition metal oxides to realize their potential in photoapplications. Hematite (α-Fe2O3) is known to form photoexcited small polarons, which limit its performance as a photoelectrocatalyst for water oxidation. Here, we report a systematic comparison of the electronic, optical and vibrational properties of hematite to those other metal oxides in the corundum crystal family that elucidates the impact of d-orbital radius on carrier-phonon coupling. Three corundum metal oxides are analyzed: α-Al2O3 (no d-electrons), α-Fe2O3 (3d), and α-Rh2O3 (4d) with a combined approach of resonance Raman spectroscopy, thermal difference optical spectroscopy, and computational modeling of electronic and vibrational states. We find that the Raman spectrum of α-Al2O3 does not change as the Raman excitation is varied across the visible region, as there is no optical absorption. In contrast, both α-Fe2O3 and α-Rh2O3 exhibit strong coupling of phonons to optical transitions at the onset of absorption, which is evidence of excitation into a polaronic state. Closely comparing the optical polaronic properties of α-Fe2O3 and α-Rh2O3, we establish that increased lattice covalency in α-Rh2O3 arising from the increased radial extension of the 4d orbitals influences which phonon modes mediate photogenerated polaron formation.

AI.tldr: The paper compares polaronic properties in corundum oxides (α-Al2O3, α-Fe2O3, α-Rh2O3) using spectroscopy and modeling, finding that d-orbital radius and lattice covalency influence phonon coupling and polaron formation in photogenerated charge carriers.
AI.motivation: Understanding polaron formation mechanisms in transition metal oxides is essential for improving their performance in photoapplications, particularly hematite (α-Fe2O3), whose performance as a photoelectrocatalyst for water oxidation is limited by photoexcited small polarons.
AI.method: Combined resonance Raman spectroscopy, thermal difference optical spectroscopy, and computational modeling of electronic and vibrational states across three corundum oxides: α-Al2O3 (no d-electrons), α-Fe2O3 (3d), and α-Rh2O3 (4d).
AI.result: α-Al2O3 shows no Raman changes across visible excitation (no optical absorption). α-Fe2O3 and α-Rh2O3 exhibit strong phonon-optical transition coupling at absorption onset, indicating polaronic excitation. Increased lattice covalency from 4d orbitals in α-Rh2O3 alters which phonon modes mediate polaron formation.
AI.conclusion: The radial extension of d-orbitals (3d vs. 4d) and resulting lattice covalency critically influence carrier-phonon coupling and the specific phonon modes involved in photogenerated polaron formation in corundum metal oxides.

title: Macroscopic Polarization and Magnetization from Cavity Vacuum Fluctuations
summary: Cavity light-matter interaction has recently emerged as a new avenue for manipulating material properties without driving fields. Here, we demonstrate that cavity vacuum fluctuations can induce macroscopic polarization (magnetization), even in materials that lack spontaneous polarization (net magnetization) in free space. Starting from the effective photon-free quantum-electrodynamics Hamiltonian, we identify all crystallographic (magnetic) point groups that allow such cavity-induced responses. We derive the form of the corresponding response tensors based on symmetry analysis, whose elements can be obtained by quantum electrodynamical density functional theory (QEDFT) calculations. As representative examples, we show that the cavity-induced polarization in $α$-quartz can be continuously controlled by rotating the cavity. For antiferromagnetic Mn$_3$Sn, we demonstrate that cavity-induced symmetry breaking generates an out-of-plane magnetization, accompanied by an anomalous Hall conductivity component that is forbidden outside the cavity. Our work establishes symmetry as a guiding principle for cavity materials engineering and provides a route for controlling polarization and magnetization through quantum vacuum fluctuations, i.e., cavity materials engineering.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that cavity vacuum fluctuations can induce macroscopic polarization and magnetization in materials that lack such properties in free space, using symmetry analysis and QEDFT calculations. Examples include α-quartz (tunable polarization) and antiferromagnetic Mn₃Sn (out-of-plane magnetization and anomalous Hall conductivity).
AI.motivation: To establish symmetry as a guiding principle for cavity materials engineering and demonstrate that quantum vacuum fluctuations in cavities can induce polarization/magnetization in materials that do not possess them intrinsically.
AI.method: Starting from the effective photon-free QED Hamiltonian, the authors identify all crystallographic (magnetic) point groups that permit cavity-induced responses, derive response tensor forms via symmetry analysis, and validate with QEDFT calculations on α-quartz and Mn₃Sn.
AI.result: Cavity-induced polarization in α-quartz is continuously controlled by cavity rotation; antiferromagnetic Mn₃Sn exhibits cavity-induced out-of-plane magnetization and an anomalous Hall conductivity component forbidden outside the cavity.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry provides a guiding principle for cavity materials engineering, and quantum vacuum fluctuations offer a controllable route for manipulating polarization and magnetization.

title: Quantum Mott semimetal in a one-dimensional Hubbard mode
summary: Mott physics in topological bands has recently attracted considerable attention, particularly in the context of twisted bilayer graphene (TBG). However, the essential ingredients for stabilizing this physics remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate a quantum Mott semimetal phase as the ground state within a one-dimensional spinful Hubbard model featuring only one orbital per unit cell, protected by inversion and particle-hole symmetries. We start from a two-orbital model where a localized $f$ orbital on the A sublattice hybridizes with a delocalized $c$ orbital on the B sublattice. Projecting the $f$-orbital Hubbard $U$ onto the active flat band yields a lattice model with Wannier orbitals centered on the B sublattice. Similar to TBG, a momentum-space scale $k_*$ emerges, setting the interaction range in the projected model to $1/k_*$. While the ground state is ferromagnetic with only the Hubbard $U$, introducing an inter-site antiferromagnetic spin coupling $J$ stabilizes a Mott semimetal$^*$ phase with a central charge $c=3$. Using exact diagonalization (ED) and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods, we show that this phase hosts a spinful Dirac fermion coexisting with a neutral spin mode -- analogous to the fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL$^*$) phase in higher dimensions. Furthermore, breaking particle-hole (PH) symmetry via dispersion transforms the Mott semimetal into a Mott insulator, which is separated from a distinct Mott insulating phase by a continuous transition with a polarization jump of $1/2$. Our work provides the first unbiased evidence of a Mott semimetal ground state and demonstrates that this 1D model captures some essential aspects of TBG physics, despite lacking a Wannier obstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a quantum Mott semimetal phase in a 1D spinful Hubbard model with inversion and particle-hole symmetries, stabilized by inter-site antiferromagnetic coupling, hosting a spinful Dirac fermion coexisting with a neutral spin mode analogous to fractionalized Fermi liquid phases.
AI.motivation: To understand the essential ingredients stabilizing Mott physics in topological bands, particularly drawing connections to twisted bilayer graphene (TBG), and to provide unbiased evidence for a Mott semimetal ground state.
AI.method: A one-dimensional spinful Hubbard model derived from a two-orbital model (localized f orbital on A sublattice hybridizing with delocalized c orbital on B sublattice). The Hubbard U is projected onto the active flat band, yielding Wannier orbitals on B sublattice with an emergent momentum-space scale k_* setting the interaction range. Exact diagonalization (ED) and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods are used.
AI.result: The ground state is ferromagnetic with only Hubbard U; adding inter-site antiferromagnetic spin coupling J stabilizes a Mott semimetal phase with central charge c=3, hosting a spinful Dirac fermion and a neutral spin mode (analogous to FL* phase). Breaking particle-hole symmetry via dispersion turns the Mott semimetal into a Mott insulator, with a continuous transition showing a polarization jump of 1/2.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first unbiased evidence of a Mott semimetal ground state and shows that the 1D model captures essential aspects of TBG physics even without Wannier obstruction.

title: Toroidal Transitions in Hydrogenic and Alkali Atoms
summary: In addition to electric and magnetic multipoles, the expansion of current density also yields toroidal terms, a lesser-known family of multipoles. A recent proposal, I. Kuprov $\textit{et al.}$, Science Adv. 8 abq6751 (2022), explores the possibility of a direct observation of optical toroidal transitions in hydrogen and alkali atoms in the presence of a large magnetic field that decouples the spin and the angular momentum of the electron. However, the difficulty of observing these transitions against the nearby electric dipole (E1) transitions were underestimated because of extra admixture coming from diamagnetic coupling. Here, we revisit the toroidal coupling in atoms, taking diamagnetic contribution into account, and discuss the technical challenges of observing toroidal coupling in atomic physics. We show that toroidal transition should be searched in transitions with low principal quantum numbers. The remaining strong electric-dipole contribution could be removed using an appropriate differential measurement.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits optical toroidal transitions in atoms, showing that previous proposals underestimated the interference from electric dipole (E1) transitions due to diamagnetic coupling. It recommends searching in low principal quantum number transitions and using differential measurement to suppress E1 background.
AI.motivation: To correct the underestimated difficulty in observing optical toroidal transitions in atoms by accounting for diamagnetic coupling contributions, and to identify practical strategies for their experimental detection.
AI.method: The authors revisit toroidal coupling in atoms by incorporating diamagnetic contributions into the theoretical framework, analyzing transition strengths and selection rules, and proposing experimental strategies such as differential measurements to isolate toroidal signals.
AI.result: Toroidal transitions should be searched in transitions with low principal quantum numbers; strong electric-dipole background can be removed via appropriate differential measurement.
AI.conclusion: Observing toroidal transitions in atoms is more challenging than previously thought due to diamagnetic coupling, but feasible with careful choice of transitions and measurement techniques.

title: Hypothesis-and-Refinement Learning of Organic Structures from Multimodal Spectroscopic Data
summary: Determining molecular structures from spectroscopic data remains fundamentally challenging because the inverse problem is intrinsically underdetermined: individual spectra are sparse, low-dimensional, and encode only partial structural evidence relative to the vast space of possible molecules. We address this challenge by formulating automated structure elucidation as a scalable hypothesis-refinement paradigm that tightly integrates spectral evidence with large-scale molecular priors. To supply structure-resolving NMR signals for multimodal learning, we construct \textbf{QM9SPIN}, a DFT-derived dataset comprising diverse 1D and 2D spectra, including J-coupling, DEPT experiments, and explicit spin--spin interactions. On this foundation, we introduce \textbf{SpectroMol}, a spectrum-to-structure model that proposes chemically valid molecular hypotheses conditioned on multimodal spectral inputs. Complementarily, we develop \textbf{MS-Mol2Mol}, a high-resolution mass-constrained molecular generator that integrates molecular formula, exact mass, and degree of unsaturation within a conditional generative prior trained on 400 million molecules, ensuring global compositional consistency and chemically realistic refinement. The integrated system achieves 93.8\% top-1 accuracy on the simulated benchmark, adapts effectively from simulated to experimental spectra with limited experimental fine-tuning, and further improves experimental predictions through mass-guided refinement, establishing a scalable route toward automated, data-driven organic structure elucidation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an automated molecular structure elucidation system that combines NMR (QM9SPIN dataset) and mass spectrometry (MS-Mol2Mol) with a spectrum-to-structure model (SpectroMol), achieving 93.8% top-1 accuracy on a simulated benchmark and effective adaptation to experimental spectra.
AI.motivation: Molecular structure determination from spectroscopic data is an underdetermined inverse problem because individual spectra are sparse and low-dimensional relative to the vast chemical space, necessitating scalable integration of spectral evidence with large-scale molecular priors.
AI.method: Construct QM9SPIN (DFT-derived dataset with diverse 1D/2D NMR spectra including J-coupling, DEPT, and spin-spin interactions); introduce SpectroMol for spectrum-to-structure prediction; develop MS-Mol2Mol as a mass-constrained molecular generator trained on 400M molecules for compositional consistency.
AI.result: 93.8% top-1 accuracy on simulated benchmark; effective adaptation from simulated to experimental spectra with limited fine-tuning; improved experimental predictions via mass-guided refinement.
AI.conclusion: The integrated system establishes a scalable, data-driven route toward automated organic structure elucidation by tightly coupling multimodal spectral evidence with large-scale generative priors.

title: Elastic Trapped States at Dislocation Defects in Scaled Coupling and Hofstadter Models
summary: Elastic topological dislocations provide a pathway for trapping elastic wave energy at internal defects, rather than being confined solely to external boundaries or corners, which are typically associated with topological insulators (TIs). However, two practical constraints persist. First, highly confined dislocation states based on conventional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) dimerization usually require a large coupling contrast and a correspondingly enlarged bandgap, which may be challenging to realize. Second, some Hamiltonians with richer topological physics often contain complex hopping terms, synthetic gauge fields or nonlocal couplings, which substantially increase the geometric complexity of experimental samples. Here, dislocation-induced trapped states are demonstrated in both a scaled coupling (SC) model and a Hofstadter model (HM) within an elastic platform. In the SC model, the trapped mode is treated as a higher localized state in the continuum rather than an in-gap mode in the SSH model. Consequently, the SC-induced dislocation can trap an enhanced mode without the requirement of an enlarged bandgap. For the HM, Householder tridiagonalization is used to map the original tight-binding Hamiltonian with complex hopping terms onto a tridiagonal matrix with only positive-real-valued nearest-neighbour (NN) hopping terms. Truncation at a weak-hopping position preserves the topological phenomena and allows a dislocation defect to be constructed from the shortened aperiodic chain. The results establish a practical route for designing highly localized modes without relying solely on bandgap enlargement or complex couplings, which advance the topological physics of elastic wave systems and promise enhanced possibilities for elastic functional devices.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates dislocation-induced trapped states in elastic systems using two models: a scaled coupling (SC) model that achieves enhanced localized modes without requiring enlarged bandgaps, and a Hofstadter model (HM) that maps complex Hamiltonians onto simple tridiagonal matrices with real-valued nearest-neighbor hopping via Householder tridiagonalization, enabling practical construction of topological dislocations.
AI.motivation: To overcome two practical constraints in elastic topological dislocations: (1) the need for large coupling contrast and enlarged bandgaps in conventional SSH models, and (2) the geometric complexity arising from complex hopping terms, synthetic gauge fields, or nonlocal couplings in richer topological Hamiltonians.
AI.method: Two approaches are used: (1) A scaled coupling (SC) model where the trapped mode is a higher localized state in the continuum (rather than an in-gap mode), eliminating the need for an enlarged bandgap. (2) A Hofstadter model (HM) where Householder tridiagonalization converts the complex tight-binding Hamiltonian into a tridiagonal matrix with only positive-real-valued nearest-neighbor hopping, allowing truncation at a weak-hopping position to preserve topological phenomena and construct dislocation defects from shortened aperiodic chains.
AI.result: The SC model traps an enhanced mode without requiring an enlarged bandgap. The HM approach successfully maps complex Hamiltonians to simple tridiagonal forms, enabling experimental realization of topological dislocations with reduced geometric complexity.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a practical route for designing highly localized modes without relying solely on bandgap enlargement or complex couplings, advancing topological physics in elastic wave systems and enabling enhanced possibilities for elastic functional devices.

title: Vanishing spin stiffness in weakly disordered two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnets
summary: We show that a small fraction of antiferromagnetic bonds qualitatively alters the long-wavelength dynamics of two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnets. Although the classical ground state remains magnetized, weak bond frustration generates logarithmically correlated spatial fluctuations of the local spin stiffness, despite the microscopic disorder being short ranged. A replica field theory calculation shows that the effective disorder strength grows under coarse graining, while the spin stiffness decreases, yielding anomalously soft magnons with a scale-dependent dynamical exponent $z > 2$. Numerical diagonalization of the semiclassical spin-wave Hamiltonian confirms the anomalous low-energy scaling. The flow is toward an infinite-disorder, zero stiffness regime.

AI.tldr: A small fraction of antiferromagnetic bonds in 2D Heisenberg ferromagnets causes logarithmically correlated spin stiffness fluctuations, leading to anomalously soft magnons with scale-dependent dynamical exponent z > 2, flowing toward an infinite-disorder, zero stiffness regime.
AI.motivation: To understand how weak bond frustration (antiferromagnetic bonds) alters the long-wavelength dynamics of 2D Heisenberg ferromagnets, despite the classical ground state remaining magnetized.
AI.method: Replica field theory calculation combined with numerical diagonalization of the semiclassical spin-wave Hamiltonian.
AI.result: Weak bond frustration generates logarithmically correlated spatial fluctuations of local spin stiffness; effective disorder strength grows under coarse graining while spin stiffness decreases, yielding anomalously soft magnons with z > 2; confirmed by numerical diagonalization showing anomalous low-energy scaling.
AI.conclusion: The system flows toward an infinite-disorder, zero stiffness regime, indicating that even a small fraction of antiferromagnetic bonds qualitatively changes the dynamics of 2D Heisenberg ferromagnets.

title: Accounting for Nanofilm Contributions in Interfacial Free Energy Calculations Using Classical Density Functional Theory
summary: Fluid nanofilms play a fundamental role in nanoscale interfacial thermodynamics, yet their treatment in classical density functional theory (cDFT) remains incomplete. We investigate nanofilm interfacial properties using a cDFT framework built upon the perturbed-chain statistical associating fluid theory (PC-SAFT) for both fluid-fluid and fluid-solid interfacial systems. Comparison with molecular simulations shows that the long-standing numerical discrepancies regarding free-standing nanofilms persist in the PC-SAFT functional predictions, supporting the view that they stem from thermal capillary-wave fluctuations rather than deficiencies of the density functional itself, as such fluctuations are inherently neglected in the mean-field approximation adopted by standard cDFT. Importantly, we establish a thermodynamically consistent framework for interfacial free energy (IFE) calculation, which explicitly incorporates nanofilm thermodynamic contributions and redefines the effective fluid volume by excluding the solid-phase region. The proposed method exhibits excellent consistency with another method based on the relationship between IFE and disjoining pressure for fluid systems, while both fluid-fluid and fluid-solid IFEs differ substantially from those predicted by the conventional method. We find that neglecting nanofilm contributions induces prominent size-dependent variations in the IFE and contact angle of hemicylindrical droplets, which is inconsistent with the extensive literature. Different methods also lead to opposite signs of the line tension for a hemispherical argon nanodroplet on a strongly lyophobic surface. The proposed framework provides a unified molecular-level basis for understanding interfacial processes involving nanofilms, including wetting, nucleation, adsorption, and other phenomena that rely on the accurate evaluation of IFEs.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a thermodynamically consistent cDFT framework based on PC-SAFT for nanofilm interfacial properties, showing that numerical discrepancies with simulations arise from capillary-wave fluctuations, not functional deficiencies, and proposing a new IFE calculation method that significantly impacts contact angles and line tension predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing cDFT treatments inadequately handle fluid nanofilms in interfacial thermodynamics, leading to numerical discrepancies with molecular simulations and inconsistent interfacial free energy (IFE) predictions.
AI.method: A cDFT framework built on PC-SAFT is used for fluid-fluid and fluid-solid interfaces. A new IFE calculation method is proposed that explicitly includes nanofilm thermodynamic contributions and redefines effective fluid volume by excluding the solid-phase region.
AI.result: Persistent numerical discrepancies between PC-SAFT cDFT and molecular simulations are attributed to thermal capillary-wave fluctuations. The proposed IFE method shows excellent consistency with the disjoining pressure-based method, while both differ substantially from conventional methods. Neglecting nanofilm contributions causes size-dependent IFE and contact angle variations. Different methods yield opposite signs of line tension for nanodroplets on strongly lyophobic surfaces.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a unified molecular-level basis for accurate evaluation of IFEs in interfacial processes involving nanofilms, such as wetting, nucleation, and adsorption.

title: Markov state models revisited: Principles and algorithms for unbiased observables
summary: Markov state models (MSMs) have become ubiquitous tools for analyzing molecular dynamics (MD) simulations because of their simple, powerful premise: although complete MD sampling may be impossible, the MSM can "stitch together" transition probabilities derived from local sampling to provide a global picture of kinetics and mechanisms. In the standard MSM framework, the available MD data is organized into a single transition matrix, which is then used to estimate all observables at a lag time chosen so the coarse-grained dynamics are approximately Markovian. This approach leads to avoidable model bias and motivates long lag times that obscure short-timescale processes of interest. In contrast, this paper shows how to obtain unbiased coarse-grained observables at any fixed lag time and for any fixed coarse-graining in the limit of infinite, properly weighted data. The central idea is to replace the single-matrix framework with two transition matrices -- one representing equilibrium dynamics and another representing source-sink recycling dynamics -- and use the correct matrix or matrices to estimate the matched dynamical observables.

AI.tldr: MSMs standard single-matrix framework introduces bias and requires long lag times. This paper replaces it with a dual-matrix framework (equilibrium dynamics + source-sink recycling dynamics) to obtain unbiased coarse-grained observables at any fixed lag time with infinite properly weighted data.
AI.motivation: Standard MSM framework uses a single transition matrix, which introduces avoidable model bias and requires long lag times that obscure short-timescale processes.
AI.method: Replace the single transition matrix with two matrices: one for equilibrium dynamics and another for source-sink recycling dynamics, using the correct matrix/matrices to estimate matched dynamical observables.
AI.result: Enables unbiased coarse-grained observables at any fixed lag time and any fixed coarse-graining in the limit of infinite, properly weighted data.
AI.conclusion: The dual-matrix framework overcomes the bias and long-lag-time limitations of standard MSMs, allowing access to short-timescale processes.

title: Nitrospinics as a platform from orbital-torque memory to artificial intelligence
summary: The exploration of energy-efficient and functional spintronics has attracted considerable attention. Orbital transport has opened new pathways for current-induced torque generation beyond the conventional spin transport based on the spin Hall effect. In addition, artificial intelligence computing has been demonstrated using spintronic devices. Further progress of these devices can be anticipated through the development of unique and functional materials beyond the existing heavy metals and topological systems with strong spin-orbit coupling. The nitride materials exhibit unique chemical, magnetic, and structural versatility, including antiferromagnetism, high thermal stability, and compatibility with diverse device architectures. Here, we propose Nitrospinics as a conceptual and functional framework that exploits nitride materials for applications ranging from orbital-torque-based spintronic devices to artificial intelligence hardware. Using Cr2N, a two-dimensional nitride MXene with an atomic layered structure, as a prototype system, we discuss how nitrogen contributes to the structural stability, the orbital torque generation, and the interfacial orbital and spin conversion. We further outline key challenges and opportunities toward establishing nitride-based materials for next-generation computing technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Nitrospinics," a framework using nitride materials (exemplified by Cr2N MXene) for energy-efficient spintronics, orbital-torque devices, and AI hardware, leveraging nitrogen's structural and functional versatility.
AI.motivation: To explore energy-efficient spintronics beyond conventional heavy-metal-based systems by exploiting nitride materials' unique chemical, magnetic, and structural properties for orbital transport and torque generation.
AI.method: Conceptual framework proposal using Cr2N (2D nitride MXene) as a prototype; analysis of nitrogen's role in structural stability, orbital torque generation, and interfacial orbital/spin conversion.
AI.result: Demonstrated that nitride materials, particularly Cr2N, can serve as platforms for orbital-torque spintronics and AI hardware, with nitrogen contributing to stability and efficient orbital-spin conversion.
AI.conclusion: Nitrospinics offers a pathway for next-generation computing technologies, though key challenges remain in establishing nitride-based materials for practical applications.

title: Anyon Crystals and Hall Crystals in a Periodic Potential
summary: We obtain integer and fractional quantum Hall crystals as ground states of a two-dimensional electron system subject to a strong perpendicular magnetic field and a periodic potential. For certain fractional states, we show that the Hall crystal can constitute an anyon crystal, with a periodic ordering of well-defined anyons. We find that the latter states can be stabilized at odd denominator Landau level filling fractions when Landau level mixing is sufficiently weak, and near half-filling of the underlying lattice. These phases are obtained from a mean-field analysis of an effective lattice model of bosons attached to an odd number of flux quanta, which transmutes their statistics to that of electrons. In boson coordinates, the Hall crystal is a supersolid: a superfluid with charge order. Under strong interactions, vortex-anti-vortex pairs spontaneously nucleate in the supersolid, realizing a crystalline state of anyons.

AI.tldr: Integer and fractional quantum Hall crystals are found as ground states in a 2D electron system under a strong magnetic field and periodic potential. Fractional Hall crystals can form anyon crystals with periodic anyon ordering, stabilized at odd denominator filling fractions with weak Landau level mixing near half-filling. The analysis uses a mean-field lattice model of bosons attached to odd flux quanta, where the Hall crystal acts as a supersolid, and strong interactions nucleate vortex-anti-vortex pairs to realize a crystalline anyon state.
AI.motivation: To investigate the possibility of integer and fractional quantum Hall crystals as ground states in a 2D electron system under a strong perpendicular magnetic field and periodic potential, and to explore the emergence of anyon crystals from such systems.
AI.method: Mean-field analysis of an effective lattice model of bosons attached to an odd number of flux quanta (statistical transmutation to electrons), examining Landau level filling fractions and interaction strengths.
AI.result: Fractional Hall crystals can form anyon crystals with periodic ordering of well-defined anyons, stabilized at odd denominator filling fractions when Landau level mixing is weak and near half-filling. In boson coordinates, the Hall crystal is a supersolid; under strong interactions, vortex-anti-vortex pairs nucleate to realize a crystalline anyon state.
AI.conclusion: Quantum Hall crystals (both integer and fractional) exist as ground states under appropriate conditions. Fractional states can host anyon crystals, offering a new platform for studying anyonic quasiparticles in ordered phases.

title: Exploring Multifunctionality in MgO-Based Magnetic Tunnel Junctions with Coexisting Magnetoresistance and Memristive Properties
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures adn 1 table. Published version of record. Published in Advanced Functional Materials 33 (2023), 2305238
summary: Magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) and memristors are two key emerging nanotechnologies that attracted significant interest for potential applications at the forefront of the digital revolution, including sensing, data storage, and non-conventional computation. The co-integration of these phenomena into a single multifunctional device is an important step toward harnessing the re-programmability of memristive systems with the high yield and varied functionality of MTJs. This study demonstrates the co-existence of magnetoresistance and memristive properties on MgO-based MTJs. These devices show a magnetoresistance with a linear response as a function of a magnetic field and no hysteresis, which are the requirements for good magnetic field sensors, as well as demonstrating a non-volatile and quasi-analogue memristive behavior as a function of an applied electrical field down to nanosecond pulses. Furthermore, by doping the oxide barrier, the memristive power consumption is lowered by 20% giving the multi-functionality of the devices a promising scalability potential. This study also shows that, memristive switching can be reversibly used to completely suppress and recover the spintronic functionalities. These results can pave the way for a seamless co-integration of memristors and spintronic devices in complex reprogrammable circuits addressing applications such as reprogrammable multifunctional field sensor arrays and neuromorphic computing.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the co-existence of magnetoresistance and memristive properties in MgO-based MTJs, enabling multifunctional devices with linear magnetic field sensing and non-volatile analog memristive switching. Doping the oxide barrier reduces power consumption by 20%, and memristive switching can reversibly suppress/recover spintronic functionality, paving the way for reprogrammable circuits in sensing and neuromorphic computing.
AI.motivation: To co-integrate magnetoresistance (from MTJs) and memristive properties into a single multifunctional device, harnessing the reprogrammability of memristive systems with the high yield and varied functionality of MTJs for advanced applications in sensing, data storage, and non-conventional computation.
AI.method: MgO-based magnetic tunnel junctions were fabricated and characterized for both magnetoresistance (linear response, no hysteresis) and memristive behavior (non-volatile, quasi-analogue switching down to nanosecond pulses). Oxide barrier doping was used to lower memristive power consumption by 20%.
AI.result: Devices exhibit linear, hysteresis-free magnetoresistance suitable for magnetic field sensors, and non-volatile quasi-analogue memristive behavior. Doping the oxide barrier reduces power consumption by 20%. Memristive switching can reversibly suppress and recover spintronic functionalities.
AI.conclusion: The co-integration of memristive and spintronic phenomena in a single device shows promising scalability and multifunctionality, enabling applications in reprogrammable field sensor arrays and neuromorphic computing.

title: Dynamical Criticality of a Machine-learning-assisted Monte Carlo algorithm for a Mean-Field Spin Glass model
summary: We critically assess the performance of an autoregressive generative neural network model by applying it to an antiferromagnetic Ising model on a random regular graph. We train the network on equilibrium configurations in the low-temperature spin-glass phase of the model and perform Monte Carlo simulations using spin configurations generated by the network. The relaxation time of the Monte Carlo simulations drastically decreases with increasing the size of the training dataset and converges to an optimal value. The dynamical exponent characterizing the growth of the optimal relaxation time as a function of the system size is slightly reduced compared to the local Monte Carlo dynamics. However, we find that the size of the training dataset to achieve the optimal performance grows much faster with the system size than the relaxation time, implying that the total training cost eventually hinders a practical use of the method at large system sizes.

AI.tldr: An autoregressive neural network is applied to an antiferromagnetic Ising model on a random regular graph. While it reduces Monte Carlo relaxation time, the training dataset size grows much faster than relaxation time with system size, limiting practical scalability.
AI.motivation: To critically assess whether autoregressive generative neural networks can practically accelerate Monte Carlo simulations in spin-glass systems, specifically by reducing relaxation times.
AI.method: Train an autoregressive neural network on equilibrium configurations from the low-temperature spin-glass phase of an antiferromagnetic Ising model on a random regular graph, then use generated configurations to seed Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.result: The Monte Carlo relaxation time decreases with larger training datasets and converges to an optimal value. The dynamical exponent for optimal relaxation time is slightly reduced compared to local Monte Carlo dynamics. However, the training dataset size required for optimal performance grows much faster with system size than the relaxation time itself.
AI.conclusion: Despite reducing relaxation time, the prohibitive growth of required training data with system size limits the practical applicability of this autoregressive neural network approach for large systems.

title: Momentum Rescaling for Collapse to a Block Ehrenfest Dynamics
summary: The Ehrenfest with collapse to a block (TAB) algorithm has recently been demonstrated to efficiently and accurately simulate nonadiabatic molecular dynamics in dense manifolds of electronic states. TAB employs an Ehrenfest force for the classical nuclei, accompanied by stochastic collapses of the electronic density matrix to account for decoherence. Energy conservation dictates that the nuclear momentum be adjusted during such a collapse. In this paper, we present a prescription for rescaling the component of the nuclear momentum that projects into the branching plane between arbitrary superposition states. This prescription yields accurate branching ratios and phase-space distributions when compared to alternative methods in which scaling is performed in the nonadiabatic coupling direction or the momentum direction. We justify this direction by deriving an effective nonadiabatic coupling vector from the localized Pechukas force during a collapse step.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new momentum rescaling prescription for the TAB algorithm that projects nuclear momentum into the branching plane between superposition states, derived from the localized Pechukas force, yielding more accurate branching ratios and phase-space distributions than existing methods.
AI.motivation: To improve the TAB algorithm's momentum rescaling during stochastic collapses of the electronic density matrix by finding a physically justified direction that ensures accurate branching ratios and phase-space distributions in nonadiabatic molecular dynamics.
AI.method: The authors derive the momentum rescaling direction from the localized Pechukas force during a collapse step, identifying the branching plane between arbitrary superposition states as the proper projection direction for nuclear momentum adjustment.
AI.result: The proposed branching-plane rescaling prescription yields accurate branching ratios and phase-space distributions, outperforming alternative methods that scale in the nonadiabatic coupling direction or momentum direction.
AI.conclusion: The branching-plane momentum rescaling derived from the Pechukas force provides a physically sound and numerically accurate approach for energy conservation in TAB simulations of nonadiabatic dynamics.

title: Localization transitions of diffusion dynamics in physical networks
summary: Network diffusion underlies many transport phenomena, with Laplacian modes setting how information spreads and relaxes. In physical networks, however, connectivity alone is not enough: node volumes introduce local dwell times that regulate how flow is stored before being propagated. Here we show that physical heterogeneity reshapes topology-driven localization, with the degree-volume ratio emerging as the relevant disorder parameter. We solve an analytical model in which ratio detuning qualitatively reorganizes the Laplacian spectrum, and demonstrate in empirical networks how degree-volume correlations shift extremal eigenmodes away from the nodes selected by topology alone. Our results reveal a general feature-rich-driven mechanism for localization control, showing that physicality non-trivially reshapes the disorder landscape governing network dynamics.

AI.tldr: Physical heterogeneity in networks, characterized by the degree-volume ratio, reshapes Laplacian mode localization by introducing node dwell times, shifting extremal eigenmodes away from topology-selected nodes.
AI.motivation: Network diffusion models typically rely on connectivity alone, but physical networks have node volumes that introduce local dwell times affecting flow propagation. The paper aims to understand how this physical heterogeneity alters localization behavior compared to purely topological predictions.
AI.method: The authors solve an analytical model where degree-volume ratio detuning reorganizes the Laplacian spectrum, and validate findings on empirical networks to show how degree-volume correlations shift extremal eigenmodes.
AI.result: The degree-volume ratio emerges as the relevant disorder parameter; physical heterogeneity qualitatively reorganizes the Laplacian spectrum and shifts extremal eigenmodes away from nodes predicted by topology alone.
AI.conclusion: Physicality non-trivially reshapes the disorder landscape governing network dynamics, revealing a feature-rich-driven mechanism for localization control beyond pure topological considerations.

title: Quantum geometry and critical temperature enhancement in MgB$_2$ superconductivity
summary: MgB$_2$, a phonon-mediated superconductor with record-high critical temperature $T_c\simeq 39$ K, is revisited to obtain a comprehensive theory of electrons, phonons, and their coupling with minimal ab initio input. We construct compact analytic models for the electronic structure, phonons, and electron-phonon coupling (EPC) of MgB$_2$. We show that strong in-plane B $sp^2$ bonding realizes an obstructed band structure whose natural description is a bond-centered kagome lattice, yielding small quasi-2D $σ$-band Fermi-surface cylinders and pronounced quantum-geometric effects. The phonon spectrum is found to closely track that of a graphene-like boron layer, but the heavy intercalated Mg atoms dominate the three acoustic branches and rigidly lift the boron modes into the optical sector, while the in-plane B-B bond-stretching mode exhibits a pronounced softening along $Γ$-A. By symmetry, this $Γ$-point bond-stretching mode is the only $Γ$ phonon that can couple to the $σ$ Fermi surface, explaining its dominant contribution to the EPC. Upon electron doping toward the doubly degenerate band edge of the $σ$ sheets, we find that a reduced density of states competes with enhanced EPC matrix elements. At light electron doping, ab initio calculations show that the EPC enhancement dominates, leading to an increase in $T_c$ (within the clean doping limit without disorder effects). Using the Gaussian approximation for the EPC tensor, we further show that this enhancement is overwhelmingly quantum geometric in origin, arising from a geometric EPC contribution of the small $σ$ Fermi surface peaked at $Γ$. Overall, our results provide a transparent, symmetry-based account of superconductivity in MgB$_2$ and suggest that quantum-geometric effects can be essential for shaping doping trends in phonon-mediated superconductors.

AI.tldr: This paper develops compact analytic models for electrons, phonons, and electron-phonon coupling in MgB₂, revealing that the superconductor's electronic structure is naturally described by a bond-centered kagome lattice with obstructed bands, and demonstrates that quantum-geometric effects dominate the doping-driven enhancement of Tc.
AI.motivation: To revisit MgB₂ (Tc ≈ 39 K) and construct a comprehensive, minimal ab initio theory of its electrons, phonons, and electron-phonon coupling, providing a transparent symmetry-based understanding of its high-temperature superconductivity and the doping dependence of Tc.
AI.method: Compact analytic models for electronic structure, phonons, and EPC are constructed. Ab initio calculations are performed. The electronic structure is mapped to a bond-centered kagome lattice. Symmetry analysis identifies the dominant EPC channel. Gaussian approximation for the EPC tensor is used to isolate quantum-geometric contributions.
AI.result: (1) The electronic structure features an obstructed band with a bond-centered kagome lattice description, yielding small quasi-2D σ-band Fermi-surface cylinders and pronounced quantum-geometric effects. (2) The phonon spectrum resembles that of graphene-like boron layers, with Mg atoms dominating acoustic branches and lifting boron modes into optical sector; the in-plane B-B bond-stretching mode softens along Γ-A. (3) By symmetry, only the Γ-point bond-stretching mode couples to the σ Fermi surface. (4) Upon electron doping, reduced DOS competes with enhanced EPC matrix elements; at light doping, EPC enhancement dominates, increasing Tc. (5) This enhancement is overwhelmingly quantum geometric in origin.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-geometric effects are essential for shaping doping trends in phonon-mediated superconductors, as demonstrated for MgB₂ where the dominant Tc enhancement upon doping arises from geometric EPC contributions of the small σ Fermi surface.

title: Raman spectroscopy of van der Waals topological magnet GdGaI
summary: We report polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy of a van der Waals compound GdGaI that is a candidate for excitonic insulators. By combining the symmetry analysis with density functional theory calculations, we identify six Raman-active phonons. The spectra exhibit only the expected anharmonic hardening down to 4 K: no additional peaks, no soft modes, and no signatures of zone folding are observed. This result indicates that any lattice distortion is below our experimental sensitivity, supporting an electronically driven origin for the band reconstruction reported by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy rather than an electron-phonon-driven mechanism. Moreover, we observe a pronounced circular dichroism of the $A_{1g}$ modes under an out-of-plane magnetic field. Based on symmetry considerations, we attribute this dichroic response to chiral $A_{1g}$ phonons with opposite angular momenta generated by spin-phonon coupling in the time-reversal-broken state. The temperature evolution of the degree of circular polarization further suggests that circularly polarized Raman spectroscopy detects the emergence of short-range antiferromagnetic correlations. Our results highlight GdGaI as a promising platform in which excitonic order, magnetism, and circularly polarized phonons can be intertwined, and demonstrate that circular-polarization Raman provides a sensitive probe of spin-phonon coupling in excitonic systems.

AI.tldr: Polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy of the excitonic insulator candidate GdGaI reveals no lattice distortion (supporting an electronically driven excitonic gap) but observes circular dichroism in A1g phonons under magnetic field, attributed to chiral phonons from spin-phonon coupling, showing that circularly polarized Raman is a sensitive probe of spin-phonon coupling in excitonic systems.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the band reconstruction in the excitonic insulator candidate GdGaI is driven by electronic or electron-phonon mechanisms, and to explore the interplay between excitonic order, magnetism, and phonon properties.
AI.method: Polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy combined with symmetry analysis and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, performed under varying temperature (down to 4 K) and out-of-plane magnetic field.
AI.result: Six Raman-active phonons identified; no additional peaks, soft modes, or zone folding signatures observed down to 4 K (only anharmonic hardening). Pronounced circular dichroism of A1g modes under out-of-plane magnetic field, attributed to chiral A1g phonons with opposite angular momenta from spin-phonon coupling. Temperature evolution of circular polarization indicates detection of short-range antiferromagnetic correlations.
AI.conclusion: The absence of lattice distortion supports an electronically driven origin for the excitonic gap over an electron-phonon-driven mechanism. GdGaI is a platform where excitonic order, magnetism, and chiral phonons intertwine, and circularly polarized Raman spectroscopy is a sensitive probe of spin-phonon coupling in such systems.

title: Coloring in anyon superconductivity
summary: The recently observed signatures of superconductivity proximate to a fractional quantum anomalous Hall (FQAH) state in a twisted MoTe$_2$ bilayer has revitalized interest in quantum phases of matter induced by anyon dynamics. Here we show how a panoply of anyon-driven phases associated with doping the lattice ${ν=2/3}$ FQAH state can be realized as competing instabilities of a Fermi surface of charge-$e/3$ "quarks" coupled to a $\mathrm{SU}(3)_{-1}$ Chern-Simons gauge field, which is dual to the more conventional $\mathrm{U}(1)_3$ Chern-Simons-Ginzburg-Landau theory of quasiholes. For example, a range of electronic superconductors emerge from color superconductivity, under which the Fermi surface experiences a pairing instability mediated by gauge fluctuations. These include SC$\star$ phases -- where superconductivity coexists with topological order -- as well as topological superconductors displaying half-integer chiral central charges when the quarks are weakly paired. One example is a topological superconductor arising from a $p+ip$ "color-valley-locked" pairing mechanism with chiral central charge $c_-=-1/2$. On the other hand, both superconducting and non-Fermi liquid phases can emerge when the quarks form an itinerant ferromagnet, polarizing the Fermi surface to a particular combination of colors. Finally, our framework naturally accommodates the possibility of anyonic bound state formation, allowing access to phases induced by doping anyons of charge $2e/3$ as opposed to $e/3$ within the same model. Our work unifies many earlier proposed anyonic phases as instabilities of a single parent quark metal phase, distilling their emergence into a competition between superconductivity and itinerant color ferromagnetism.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that doping the ν=2/3 FQAH state in twisted MoTe₂ bilayer leads to a variety of anyon-driven phases (superconductors, topological superconductors, non-Fermi liquids) that emerge as competing instabilities of a Fermi surface of charge-e/3 "quarks" coupled to an SU(3)₋₁ Chern-Simons gauge field, unifying many previously proposed anyonic phases under a single framework of competition between superconductivity and itinerant color ferromagnetism.
AI.motivation: Recent experimental signatures of superconductivity proximate to a fractional quantum anomalous Hall (FQAH) state in twisted MoTe₂ bilayer have revitalized interest in quantum phases driven by anyon dynamics, motivating a unified theoretical understanding of the possible phases arising from doping the FQAH state.
AI.method: The authors develop a dual description of the ν=2/3 FQAH state: a Fermi surface of charge-e/3 "quarks" coupled to an SU(3)₋₁ Chern-Simons gauge field, which is dual to the conventional U(1)₃ Chern-Simons-Ginzburg-Landau theory of quasiholes. They analyze competing instabilities of this parent quark metal phase.
AI.result: They find: (1) SC⋆ phases where superconductivity coexists with topological order; (2) topological superconductors with half-integer chiral central charges (e.g., c₋=-1/2 from p+ip "color-valley-locked" pairing); (3) superconducting and non-Fermi liquid phases from itinerant color ferromagnetism; (4) phases from anyonic bound states of charge 2e/3.
AI.conclusion: The work unifies many earlier proposed anyonic phases as instabilities of a single parent quark metal phase, distilling their emergence into a competition between superconductivity and itinerant color ferromagnetism.

title: Nuclear Quantum Effects as a Denoising Problem
summary: Nuclear quantum effects are rigorously captured by imaginary-time path integrals, which map the quantum Boltzmann distribution onto a ring polymer of classical replicas. Yet the nuclear masses, the coupling to the environment, and the boundary conditions of the path remain hard-wired in the simulation or the trained model, even though this quantum context enters the path measure only through a quadratic action known in closed form. Here we show that a denoiser trained on classical Boltzmann statistics alone, composed at sampling time with an analytic Gaussian component carrying the entire quantum context, yields the quantum Boltzmann distribution of the nuclei. Such a composition exists and is exact whenever the training noise does not exceed the intrinsic quantum uncertainty of the target ensemble, and it is invariant across all quantum contexts admitted by this bound. We show exact transfer across temperature, isotopic mass, dissipation strength, and the boundary conditions of the path in theory and in numerical experiments, without retraining. The last yields the end-to-end displacement and momentum distributions of a tagged nucleus from open imaginary-time paths. The same invariance extends in principle to the permuted boundary conditions of bosonic exchange, with the identical denoiser. In this view, the noise of generative modeling and the quantum fluctuations of the nuclei are two faces of the same quadratic structure.

AI.tldr: A single denoiser trained on classical Boltzmann statistics can be composed with an analytic Gaussian component to exactly generate quantum Boltzmann distributions of nuclei, enabling zero-shot transfer across temperature, mass, dissipation, and boundary conditions.
AI.motivation: Nuclear quantum effects are captured via imaginary-time path integrals (ring polymers), but traditional simulations and trained models have the quantum context (mass, temperature, dissipation, boundary conditions) hard-wired, requiring retraining for each new condition.
AI.method: A denoiser trained solely on classical Boltzmann statistics is composed at sampling time with an analytic Gaussian component that encodes the quantum context (quadratic action). This composition is exact when training noise ≤ intrinsic quantum uncertainty of the target ensemble, and is invariant across all quantum contexts within that bound.
AI.result: Demonstrated exact zero-shot transfer across temperature, isotopic mass, dissipation strength, and boundary conditions (including open paths). Also extends to permuted boundary conditions for bosonic exchange without retraining. Numerical experiments confirm end-to-end displacement and momentum distributions of tagged nuclei.
AI.conclusion: The noise in generative modeling and quantum fluctuations of nuclei share the same quadratic structure, enabling a universal denoiser that separates classical Boltzmann training from quantum context injection.

title: Weakly Nonlinear Dynamics of Unstable Modes in Jammed Amorphous Solids
summary: We investigate the structural evolution in jammed amorphous solids by analyzing the eigenmodes of a generalized Hessian matrix that incorporates spatial modulation via wave numbers. Unlike the conventional Hessian, this generalized formulation captures linearly unstable modes through a Fourier-based extension of the Hessian matrix, enabling us to study responses beyond the mechanically stable regime. We demonstrate that the excitation of unstable eigenmodes leads to structural rearrangements independent of the initial perturbation by the simulation. Furthermore, we derive a weakly nonlinear amplitude equation to describe the growth and saturation of these unstable modes, analogous to the Landau equation. Our framework provides a pathway to understand instability-driven configuration changes in disordered solids.

AI.tldr: This paper studies structural evolution in jammed amorphous solids using a generalized Hessian matrix with spatial modulation via wave numbers, revealing that unstable eigenmodes drive structural rearrangements independent of initial perturbation, and derives a weakly nonlinear amplitude equation (analogous to Landau equation) to describe mode growth and saturation.
AI.motivation: To understand instability-driven structural changes in disordered solids beyond the mechanically stable regime, which conventional Hessian analysis cannot capture.
AI.method: The authors analyze eigenmodes of a generalized Hessian matrix that incorporates Fourier-based spatial modulation via wave numbers, extending analysis beyond stable regimes. They derive a weakly nonlinear amplitude equation analogous to the Landau equation.
AI.result: Excitation of unstable eigenmodes leads to structural rearrangements that are independent of the initial perturbation. The growth and saturation of these modes can be described by the derived nonlinear amplitude equation.
AI.conclusion: The generalized Hessian framework offers a pathway to understand instability-driven configuration changes in disordered solids.

title: Power-Law Suppression of Superfluid Stiffness in High-Kinetic-Inductance NbN Films
summary: Disorder is a powerful route to high kinetic inductance in superconducting ultrathin films, enabling compact high-impedance quantum circuits. This functionality, however, comes at the cost of reduced phase rigidity and potentially anomalous electrodynamics. Here, we use NbN microwave resonators with thicknesses down to 2.8 nm and sheet kinetic inductance up to 300 pH per square to probe how this trade-off reshapes the superconducting response. In the thinnest films, transport shows signatures of a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, while the microwave response reveals a pronounced low-temperature power-law suppression of the superfluid stiffness, inconsistent with Mattis-Bardeen theory. With increasing thickness, this anomalous regime is progressively suppressed, marking a continuous crossover toward conventional, gap-dominated electrodynamics. Cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy reveals a nanocrystalline twin-domain structure, pointing to oriented microstructural disorder as a crucial factor in the observed response. Overall, the crossover is governed by the ratio of superfluid stiffness to pairing energy, Theta(0)/Tc, identifying this ratio as a parameter governing the boundary between phase-fluctuation-dominated and gap-dominated superconducting electrodynamics in disordered nanofilms.

AI.tldr: NbN microwave resonators with thicknesses down to 2.8 nm show a crossover from phase-fluctuation-dominated (BKT-like, power-law suppression of superfluid stiffness) to gap-dominated electrodynamics, governed by the ratio Θ(0)/Tc, with microstructural disorder (nanocrystalline twin domains) as a key factor.
AI.motivation: To understand how disorder-induced high kinetic inductance in superconducting ultrathin films leads to reduced phase rigidity and anomalous electrodynamics, and to characterize the trade-off between high impedance and superconducting coherence.
AI.method: NbN microwave resonators of varying thickness (down to 2.8 nm) were fabricated and characterized via transport measurements and microwave response, with cross-sectional TEM to probe microstructure.
AI.result: Thinnest films exhibit BKT transition signatures and low-temperature power-law suppression of superfluid stiffness (deviating from Mattis-Bardeen theory); this anomalous regime is progressively suppressed with increasing thickness. The crossover is governed by Θ(0)/Tc.
AI.conclusion: The ratio of superfluid stiffness to pairing energy, Θ(0)/Tc, identifies the boundary between phase-fluctuation-dominated and gap-dominated electrodynamics in disordered nanofilms.

title: Dynamical and Optimization Trade-offs of Levi--Civita Coordinates for Learned Close-Encounter Dynamics
summary: Classical regularization removes the binary-collision singularity from the Kepler problem, but its value as a representation for learned Hamiltonian dynamics has not been systematically isolated. We compare Cartesian and planar Levi--Civita formulations of a perturbed Kepler system with a smooth quadrupole potential. With the perturbation supplied analytically, a Levi--Civita Hamiltonian splitting holds the maximum relative energy error near $2.1\times10^{-5}$ through eccentricity $e=0.99$, while the Cartesian splitting becomes unstable. This advantage persists at matched physical horizon and force-evaluation budget, where the regularized baseline is $3\times10^{-5}$, about $4.7$--$8.3$ orders of magnitude below the Cartesian arm depending on eccentricity. In held-out high-eccentricity tests with matched sampling, regularized models produce finite rollouts in $40/40$ runs versus $0/40$ for Cartesian. However, the fixed-shell construction supplies the regularized model with the exact initial orbit energy, and survival still carries $\mathcal{O}(1)$ energy error. Four neural residual objectives fail to approach the analytic result. Exact-feature controls show that the regularized residual is a four-monomial degree-6 polynomial that a direct least-squares solve fits to the baseline. The remaining exact-feature gap is due to severe raw-basis ill-conditioning: orthogonalization restores baseline fitting for L-BFGS in two iterations. Small MLPs remain at $\mathcal{O}(1)$ rollout error even after gauge symmetrization. Levi--Civita coordinates therefore improve dynamical conditioning while worsening raw-basis optimization conditioning; accurate neural residual learning remains unresolved. This is a controlled falsification-plus-trade-off study, not a solution to learned close-encounter dynamics.

AI.tldr: This study compares Cartesian and Levi-Civita (regularized) formulations for learning Hamiltonian dynamics of a perturbed Kepler system. The regularized approach achieves far superior stability and energy conservation (by 4.7–8.3 orders of magnitude) and survives all high-eccentricity rollouts vs. 0/40 for Cartesian. However, neural residual learning fails to approach the analytic regularized baseline due to severe raw-basis ill-conditioning, and small MLPs yield O(1) rollout errors even with gauge symmetrization.
AI.motivation: To systematically isolate the value of classical regularization (Levi-Civita) for learned Hamiltonian dynamics, which had not been previously studied in the context of neural network-based learning.
AI.method: Compare Cartesian vs. planar Levi-Civita formulations of a perturbed Kepler system (with smooth quadrupole potential). Uses Hamiltonian splitting, matched physical horizon and force-evaluation budget, held-out high-eccentricity tests, fixed-shell construction, exact-feature controls, least-squares solves, orthogonalization, and small MLPs with gauge symmetrization.
AI.result: Levi-Civita splitting holds ~2.1×10⁻⁵ relative energy error through e=0.99 vs. Cartesian instability. Regularized baseline is 3×10⁻⁵, 4.7–8.3 orders of magnitude better than Cartesian. Regularized models produce 40/40 finite rollouts (0/40 Cartesian). However, neural residual objectives fail to approach the analytic result; exact-feature gap exists due to raw-basis ill-conditioning; small MLPs remain at O(1) rollout error.
AI.conclusion: Levi-Civita coordinates improve dynamical conditioning but worsen raw-basis optimization conditioning. Accurate neural residual learning of regularized dynamics remains an unresolved problem. The paper is a controlled falsification-plus-trade-off study, not a solution to learned close-encounter dynamics.

title: Synergistic Interface Stability and High Room-Temperature Ionic Conductivity for Wide-Temperature All-Solid-State Batteries Based on Li6+xSixSb1-xS5I Electrolytes
summary: Solid-state lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) are increasingly recognized for their exceptional energy density and safety. However, their widespread adoption is challenged by persistent issues such as thermal and electrochemical instability, dendrite formation, and limited compatibility with high-voltage cathodes. Sulfide-based solid electrolytes (SEs), particularly iodide argyrodites, offer outstanding ionic conductivity and stability; however, their practical application is constrained by the formation of space-charge layers, slow ion transport, and susceptibility to dendrite penetration. To address these challenges, we synthesized a novel Li6.6Si0.6Sb0.4S5I argyrodite electrolyte via ball milling and heat treatment, achieving a remarkable room-temperature ionic conductivity of 9.9 mS cm^-1. The electrolyte was integrated with a LiNbO3-coated LiNi0.7Co0.1Mn0.2O2 cathode to form an all-solid-state battery, which demonstrated an initial discharge capacity of 171.2 mAh g^-1, retained 84.2% of its capacity after 200 cycles at 0.5C, and maintained stable cycling across a broad temperature range from -20 degrees C to 60 degrees C. Our study shows that tailored electrolyte composition and a composite cathode configuration significantly enhance cycling stability and improve interfacial protection. These findings highlight the potential of Si-doped antimony-type iodide argyrodites for next-generation high-performance all-solid-state batteries, offering durable operation under diverse thermal conditions.

AI.tldr: A novel Li6.6Si0.6Sb0.4S5I argyrodite electrolyte was synthesized via ball milling and heat treatment, achieving 9.9 mS cm^-1 ionic conductivity at room temperature. When integrated with a LiNbO3-coated NCM cathode, the all-solid-state battery delivered 171.2 mAh g^-1 initial capacity, retained 84.2% after 200 cycles at 0.5C, and operated stably from -20°C to 60°C.
AI.motivation: Solid-state LIBs face challenges of thermal/electrochemical instability, dendrite formation, and poor compatibility with high-voltage cathodes. Sulfide SEs, especially iodide argyrodites, suffer from space-charge layers, slow ion transport, and dendrite penetration, motivating the need for improved electrolyte compositions.
AI.method: Synthesized Li6.6Si0.6Sb0.4S5I argyrodite via ball milling and heat treatment; integrated with LiNbO3-coated LiNi0.7Co0.1Mn0.2O2 (NCM) cathode to form an all-solid-state battery.
AI.result: Room-temperature ionic conductivity of 9.9 mS cm^-1; initial discharge capacity of 171.2 mAh g^-1; 84.2% capacity retention after 200 cycles at 0.5C; stable cycling from -20°C to 60°C.
AI.conclusion: Tailored electrolyte composition and composite cathode configuration enhance cycling stability and interfacial protection. Si-doped antimony-type iodide argyrodites show strong potential for next-generation high-performance all-solid-state batteries with durable operation under diverse thermal conditions.

title: Optical Magnetic Switching in Odd-Parity Magnets with Spin-Orbit Coupling
comment: 5+5 pages, 11 figures, Submitted to a journal
summary: $p$-wave magnets exhibit odd-parity spin polarization in momentum space, with spin splitting that reverses under $\vec{k}\rightarrow -\vec{k}$, while preserving zero net magnetization. Here we show that, in odd-parity magnets with spin-orbit coupling, elliptically polarized light generates a momentum-independent spin-dependent term that dynamically switches a zero-net-magnetization $p$-wave state into a finite spin-polarized state. The Floquet-engineered bands also acquire a nonzero Chern number whose sign is controlled by the light polarization. For $f$-wave magnets, circularly polarized light induces a net out-of-plane magnetization, offering a direct experimental signature. Our results establish light as an efficient means of controlling magnetic states, with potential applications in spintronics and quantum information.

AI.tldr: Light can switch p-wave and f-wave magnets from zero-net-magnetization states to finite spin-polarized states via Floquet engineering, with light polarization controlling the induced Chern number and magnetization direction.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that elliptically/circularly polarized light can dynamically control magnetic states in odd-parity magnets (p-wave and f-wave) that have zero net magnetization, enabling optical switching of magnetic order.
AI.method: Floquet engineering analysis for odd-parity magnets with spin-orbit coupling under elliptically polarized light; calculating Floquet-engineered band structures, Chern numbers, and induced magnetization.
AI.result: Elliptically polarized light generates a momentum-independent spin-dependent term that switches p-wave magnets to finite spin-polarized states. The Floquet bands acquire nonzero Chern numbers controlled by light polarization. Circularly polarized light induces net out-of-plane magnetization in f-wave magnets.
AI.conclusion: Light is an efficient, controllable means of switching magnetic states in odd-parity magnets, with applications in spintronics and quantum information.

title: Motility destabilizes an absorbing-state flock
summary: Activity, when it takes the form of motility, is generally seen to promote order in many-body systems. Here we present a one-dimensional lattice model that, in the non-motile limit, exhibits absorbing ferromagnetic states. When activity is introduced through biased motility, these absorbing state are destabilised and the system instead undergoes a transition from an ordered flock to a disordered state as the alignment strength is decreased. A finite-size scaling analysis of physical quantities reveals a continuous transition with critical exponents satisfying the hyperscaling relation in one dimension, providing quantitative evidence for the activity-induced disorder.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 1D lattice model where, in the non-motile limit, absorbing ferromagnetic states exist. Introducing biased motility destabilizes these states, causing a transition from an ordered flock to a disordered state as alignment strength decreases. Finite-size scaling reveals a continuous transition with critical exponents satisfying the hyperscaling relation in 1D, providing quantitative evidence for activity-induced disorder.
AI.motivation: To investigate how activity (biased motility) affects ordered states in many-body systems, specifically challenging the common notion that motility promotes order by showing that activity can instead induce disorder.
AI.method: A one-dimensional lattice model with biased motility is studied. In the non-motile limit, the system exhibits absorbing ferromagnetic states. Activity is introduced through biased motility, and finite-size scaling analysis of physical quantities is performed to characterize the phase transition.
AI.result: Biased motility destabilizes the absorbing ferromagnetic states. The system undergoes a continuous transition from an ordered flock to a disordered state as alignment strength decreases. Critical exponents satisfy the hyperscaling relation in one dimension.
AI.conclusion: Activity-induced disorder is quantitatively established: contrary to the common view that motility promotes order, biased motility can destroy ordered absorbing states and drive a continuous phase transition to disorder.

title: Stacking-tuned superconductivity and competing charge-density-wave states in NbSe$_2$
summary: Layer stacking provides a powerful yet underexplored route for reshaping collective quantum order in van der Waals materials. Here we use high-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy to show that the stacking sequence alone can qualitatively transform the charge density and superconducting orders in NbSe$_2$, while preserving the same in-plane atomic structure. Comparing the 4Ha and 2H polytypes, we find that, unlike the ubiquitous triangular incommensurate $3Q^\mathrm{I}$ order of 2H-NbSe$_2$, 4Ha-NbSe$_2$ hosts two competing CDW states with no measurable correlation with local strain: a unidirectional commensurate $1Q^\mathrm{C}$ phase and a triangular incommensurate $3Q^\mathrm{I}$ phase, with $Q^\mathrm{I}=Q^\mathrm{C}+δ$. We introduce a phase-resolved analysis that directly maps the gradient of the CDW phases and reveals vortices bound to the $1Q^\mathrm{C}$ - $3Q^\mathrm{I}$ phase boundaries. These vortices accommodate the momentum mismatch $δ$ through abrupt $2π$ phase slips, providing a mechanism by which distinct charge orders coexist. Superconductivity is also reshaped by stacking, while both polytypes exhibit multiband pairing.

AI.tldr: Stacking sequence in NbSe₂ polytypes (4Ha vs 2H) qualitatively transforms charge density wave (CDW) orders and superconductivity. 4Ha-NbSe₂ hosts coexisting unidirectional commensurate 1Q^C and triangular incommensurate 3Q^I CDW phases, with phase-resolved mapping revealing vortices at boundaries that accommodate momentum mismatch via 2π phase slips. Superconductivity is also reshaped by stacking while preserving multiband pairing.
AI.motivation: To explore how layer stacking sequence alone, without altering in-plane atomic structure, can qualitatively reshape collective quantum orders (charge density and superconductivity) in van der Waals materials, specifically NbSe₂.
AI.method: High-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/S) to compare 4Ha and 2H polytypes of NbSe₂; phase-resolved analysis to map CDW phase gradients and identify vortices at phase boundaries.
AI.result: 4Ha-NbSe₂ exhibits two competing CDW states (1Q^C and 3Q^I) with no correlation to local strain, unlike the single 3Q^I order in 2H-NbSe₂. Phase vortices bound to boundaries accommodate momentum mismatch δ via 2π phase slips. Superconductivity shows stacking-dependent reshaping while retaining multiband pairing.
AI.conclusion: Stacking sequence is a powerful tuning knob for collective quantum phases in van der Waals materials, enabling coexistence of distinct charge orders through phase-vortex mechanisms and altering superconducting properties.

title: Bayesian Inference: Kernel-Based Model for Surface Temperature Reconstruction in Ice Borehole Thermometry
summary: Reconstructing past surface temperature from shallow ice borehole temperature profiles requires solving an ill-posed inverse problem while quantifying uncertainties arising from measurements and prior assumptions. Bayesian formulations enable probabilistic reconstruction of surface temperature histories and uncertainty quantification. Existing reversible jump-Markov chain Monte Carlo approach based on adaptive piecewise-linear surface temperature models can, however, be computationally demanding. Here, we introduce a kernel-based surface temperature model that enables the use of a parallel ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for efficient exploration of the solution space and quantification of the posterior.
