Using synthetic experiments, we investigate the effects of kernel configuration, measurement uncertainty, measurement density, and temporal smearing on reconstruction performance. We find that reconstruction quality is largely insensitive to the number of kernels once the kernel basis is sufficiently dense. Reducing measurement uncertainty substantially improves reconstructions, whereas increasing the number of borehole temperature measurements provides only marginal benefit. Finally, we evaluate the method using realistic surrogate climate histories that combine long-term temperature changes with stochastic climate variability. The kernel-based surface temperature model cannot represent short-term variability and therefore cannot fully explain the realistic measurements, highlighting the need to account for this approximation uncertainty. The likelihood is adapted to include the approximation uncertainty of the surface temperature model, yielding robust reconstructions with reliable posterior uncertainties. Overall, our results demonstrate that kernel-based Bayesian inversion provides an efficient framework for shallow ice borehole based climate reconstructions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a kernel-based Bayesian inversion method for reconstructing past surface temperatures from shallow ice borehole data. It uses a parallel ensemble MCMC sampler for efficient uncertainty quantification, showing that reconstruction quality is robust to kernel count but sensitive to measurement uncertainty, and that accounting for approximation uncertainty from the kernel's inability to capture short-term variability yields reliable posterior uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Existing reversible jump-Markov chain Monte Carlo approaches for reconstructing past surface temperature from shallow ice borehole profiles are computationally demanding. The authors aim to develop a more efficient framework for probabilistic reconstruction and uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: The authors propose a kernel-based surface temperature model combined with a parallel ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler. They conduct synthetic experiments varying kernel configuration, measurement uncertainty, measurement density, and temporal smearing. They also test on realistic surrogate climate histories and adapt the likelihood to include approximation uncertainty from the kernel model's inability to represent short-term variability.
AI.result: Reconstruction quality is largely insensitive to kernel number once the kernel basis is sufficiently dense. Reducing measurement uncertainty substantially improves reconstructions, while increasing measurement density provides only marginal benefit. The kernel model cannot represent short-term climate variability, but adapting the likelihood to include this approximation uncertainty yields robust reconstructions with reliable posterior uncertainties.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-based Bayesian inversion provides an efficient framework for shallow ice borehole-based climate reconstructions, offering computational advantages over previous reversible jump-MCMC methods while maintaining robust uncertainty quantification.

title: Chiral Magnetic Conductivity in the Tight-Binding Model of Dirac Semimetals
summary: We consider the typical tight - binding model of Dirac semimetal in the presence of both magnetic and electric fields. The electric conductivity reveals dependence on magnetic field. We calculate this dependence in the limit of strong magnetic field, when the given model is described effectively by the one - dimensional SSH model because the dynamics in the plane orthogonal to magnetic field is reduced to that of the lowest Landau level (LLL). Considering the small temperature limit we take into account dissipation due to scattering on impurities. The corresponding dissipation rate is calculated explicitly. The obtained results confirm that the source of the magnetoconductivity in this system is chiral magnetic effect.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the magnetoconductivity of a Dirac semimetal under strong magnetic and electric fields, finding that the chiral magnetic effect is the source of the observed behavior, using an effective one-dimensional SSH model derived from the lowest Landau level approximation with impurity scattering.
AI.motivation: To understand the dependence of electric conductivity on magnetic field in Dirac semimetals and to confirm that the chiral magnetic effect is responsible for the magnetoconductivity.
AI.method: The tight-binding model of a Dirac semimetal with both magnetic and electric fields is considered. In the strong magnetic field limit, the model reduces to an effective one-dimensional SSH model due to confinement to the lowest Landau level. The small temperature limit is considered, and dissipation from impurity scattering is included, with the dissipation rate calculated explicitly.
AI.result: The calculated magnetoconductivity dependence on magnetic field confirms that the chiral magnetic effect is the source of the magnetoconductivity in this system.
AI.conclusion: The chiral magnetic effect is identified as the origin of magnetoconductivity in Dirac semimetals under strong magnetic fields, validated through explicit calculation of the dissipation rate from impurity scattering in the effective SSH model.

title: Analytical Retrieval of Material Parameters in Monolayer Transition-Metal Dichalcogenides Based on a Solvable Exciton Model
summary: We develop an analytical procedure to retrieve fundamental material parameters of monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides from optical and magneto-optical exciton spectra, based on the solvable modified Kratzer model. The proposed retrieval procedure naturally consists of two complementary stages. In the first stage, explicit inversion formulas determine the quasiparticle bandgap, effective screening parameter, and energy scaling factor directly from the experimentally measured energies of the three lowest excitonic states, from which the screening length is subsequently obtained. In the second stage, an analytical expression for the magnetic-field dependence of the exciton energies independently yields the reduced exciton mass, from which the surrounding dielectric constant is then calculated. Once the complete set of material parameters has been retrieved, the framework analytically predicts the diamagnetic coefficients, exciton radii, and complete magnetoexciton spectra without introducing additional fitting parameters or matrix diagonalization. The method is applied to a broad range of experimental samples for WSe$_2$, WS$_2$, MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and MoTe$_2$ monolayers embedded in different dielectric environments. The retrieved material parameters are in good agreement with independent experimental measurements and previous Rytova--Keldysh (RK) calculations, while the predicted excitonic properties accurately reproduce available magneto-optical observations. The proposed analytical theory provides an efficient, physically transparent alternative to conventional numerical fitting procedures and offers an effective tool for the rapid characterization of two-dimensional semiconductors via excitonic spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an analytical method based on the modified Kratzer model to retrieve fundamental material parameters (bandgap, screening, mass, dielectric constant) of monolayer TMDs from optical/magneto-optical exciton spectra, validated across multiple materials and dielectric environments.
AI.motivation: To provide an efficient, physically transparent analytical alternative to conventional numerical fitting procedures for extracting material parameters of 2D semiconductors from excitonic spectroscopy.
AI.method: A two-stage analytical retrieval procedure based on the solvable modified Kratzer model: Stage 1 uses explicit inversion formulas from the three lowest excitonic energies to obtain quasiparticle bandgap, screening parameter, and energy scaling factor; Stage 2 uses analytical magnetic-field dependence of exciton energies to obtain reduced exciton mass and dielectric constant.
AI.result: Applied to WSe₂, WS₂, MoS₂, MoSe₂, and MoTe₂ monolayers in various dielectric environments. Retrieved parameters agree well with independent measurements and Rytova-Keldysh calculations; predicted excitonic properties accurately reproduce magneto-optical observations.
AI.conclusion: The analytical theory offers an efficient, physically transparent alternative to numerical fitting, enabling rapid characterization of 2D semiconductors via excitonic spectroscopy without additional fitting parameters or matrix diagonalization.

title: Twisting-operator approach to identifying gaplessness in SU($N$) fermionic systems
summary: We propose a general necessary condition for a spinful fermion chain with SU(2) spin-rotation symmetry to be gapped. Specifically, we prove that the expectation value of a properly defined fermionic twisting operator asymptotically approaches unity in any gapped phase with finite ground-state degeneracy, with finite-size corrections bounded by $\mathscr{O}(1/L)$. Consequently, a non-unity value in the thermodynamic limit provides a sufficient criterion for identifying gapless fermion chains. We confirm this criterion using the $s$-wave Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) Hamiltonian and determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) simulations of interacting Hubbard models. We further extend the twisting-operator approach to SU($N$)-symmetric fermionic systems, where the gapped ground-state sector must be SU($N$)-singlet and $\langle \hat{\mathcal{U}}^M\rangle=1+\mathscr{O}(1/L)$ by a fermionic twisting operator $\hat{\mathcal{U}}$ with a suitably chosen integer $M$.

AI.tldr: A fermionic twisting operator is proven to approach unity in gapped phases of SU(2)-symmetric fermion chains, providing a necessary condition for gappedness and a sufficient criterion for gaplessness, with extensions to SU(N)-symmetric systems.
AI.motivation: To establish a general necessary condition for spinful fermion chains with SU(2) symmetry to be gapped, enabling a rigorous diagnostic to distinguish gapped vs. gapless phases.
AI.method: Proof that a fermionic twisting operator's expectation value asymptotically approaches unity in any gapped phase with finite ground-state degeneracy, with O(1/L) finite-size corrections; validated via s-wave BCS Hamiltonian and DQMC simulations of Hubbard models; extended to SU(N)-symmetric systems with a suitably chosen integer M.
AI.result: The twisting operator criterion correctly identifies gapped vs. gapless phases in the BCS and Hubbard models; the condition holds for SU(N)-symmetric systems where the gapped ground state must be an SU(N) singlet.
AI.conclusion: A non-unity twisting operator expectation value in the thermodynamic limit is a sufficient criterion for gapless fermion chains; the approach generalizes to SU(N) symmetry.

title: Spin-Consistency Constraints in Noncollinear Tensor TDA
summary: TDDFT for open-shell systems, whether spin-conserving or spin-flip, has long suffered from spin contamination. This problem arises because the single-excitation space built upon a single Kohn-Sham determinant is not spin-complete. Adopting spin tensor reference states therefore offers an elegant and promising route to resolving this issue. In this work, we revisit the tensor TDDFT equations within the Tamm-Dancoff approximation (TDA) from a noncollinear perspective. We show that, for S = 1/2 reference states, the internal consistency of the spin tensor formulation can, with the aid of the zero-excitation-energy theorem, be recast as a set of constraints that the exchange-correlation kernel must satisfy. Standard noncollinear functionals, however, generally fail to meet these constraints. To address this, we propose a kernel reconstruction scheme that is independent of the specific functional form and free of empirical parameters. This scheme enforces the required constraints, restoring internal consistency in the full spin tensor structure, with spin adaptation following as a natural consequence. Furthermore, when extended to tensor reference states with other values of S, such as S = 1 for the oxygen molecule, the scheme eliminates the so-called artifact states, namely solutions with severely underestimated excitation energies. In addition, the scheme allows the target states that ROKS reference states aim to describe to be expressed and computed, at the TDA level, within the same unified framework as other states, a capability that spin-adapted spin-conserving TDDFT has so far lacked.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses spin contamination in TDDFT for open-shell systems by revisiting tensor TDDFT within the Tamm-Dancoff approximation. The authors derive constraints for the exchange-correlation kernel from internal consistency and the zero-excitation-energy theorem, propose a functional-independent kernel reconstruction scheme that enforces these constraints, and demonstrate that this eliminates artifact states and unifies the description of target states typically handled by ROKS.
AI.motivation: Spin contamination has long plagued TDDFT for open-shell systems (both spin-conserving and spin-flip) because the single-excitation space built on a single Kohn-Sham determinant is not spin-complete. The authors aim to resolve this by revisiting the spin tensor formulation.
AI.method: The authors revisit tensor TDDFT equations within the Tamm-Dancoff approximation (TDA) from a noncollinear perspective. They show that for S=1/2 reference states, internal consistency combined with the zero-excitation-energy theorem yields constraints on the exchange-correlation kernel. They then propose a kernel reconstruction scheme that is functional-independent and parameter-free to enforce these constraints.
AI.result: Standard noncollinear functionals fail to meet the derived constraints. The proposed reconstruction scheme restores internal consistency in the full spin tensor structure, with spin adaptation emerging naturally. For S=1 reference states (e.g., O₂), the scheme eliminates artifact states (severely underestimated excitation energies). It also enables target states of ROKS reference states to be expressed and computed within the same unified framework at the TDA level—a capability previously missing in spin-adapted spin-conserving TDDFT.
AI.conclusion: The kernel reconstruction scheme provides a systematic, functional-independent, and parameter-free solution to spin contamination in tensor TDDFT, removing artifact states and unifying the description of target states across different spin reference states.

title: Logarithmic scaling correction in quench dynamics of the J1-J2 Potts model
summary: In conventional quench dynamics governed by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM), the defect density generally decays as a pure power law of the quench rate. However, the KZM scaling of the two-dimensional (2D) XY model with topological phase transitions features prominent logarithmic corrections. Nevertheless, it remains unclear whether such logarithmic scaling corrections emerge in discrete-spin systems that host two successive topological phase transitions under thermal quenches. This work investigates the J1-J2 antiferromagnetic Potts model and constructs its equilibrium phase diagram. Based on the temperature ranges of the paramagnetic phase, quasi-long-range ordered (QLRO) phase, long-range ordered phase, and zero-temperature ground state, we design four quench protocols with distinct temperature intervals. Our results demonstrate that quenches terminating in the QLRO phase exhibit logarithmically corrected KZM scaling of the excess energy density, consistent with the dynamical universality class of the 2D XY model. In contrast, quenches ending in the LRO phase, including both finite-temperature and zero-temperature protocols, follow conventional power-law scaling. Our results clearly uncover the characteristic scaling corrections of the J1-J2 Potts model and offer theoretical guidance for future experimental investigations of KZM via photonic simulation platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the Kibble-Zurek mechanism (KZM) scaling in the J1-J2 antiferromagnetic Potts model, which hosts two successive topological phase transitions. It finds that quenches ending in the quasi-long-range ordered (QLRO) phase exhibit logarithmically corrected KZM scaling of excess energy density (consistent with the 2D XY model), while quenches ending in the long-range ordered (LRO) phase follow conventional power-law scaling.
AI.motivation: To understand whether logarithmic scaling corrections to the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, previously observed in the 2D XY model with topological phase transitions, also emerge in discrete-spin systems that host two successive topological phase transitions under thermal quenches.
AI.method: The work constructs the equilibrium phase diagram of the J1-J2 antiferromagnetic Potts model. Based on the temperature ranges of the paramagnetic phase, QLRO phase, LRO phase, and zero-temperature ground state, four quench protocols with distinct temperature intervals are designed and simulated.
AI.result: Quenches terminating in the QLRO phase exhibit logarithmically corrected KZM scaling of the excess energy density, consistent with the 2D XY model's dynamical universality class. Quenches ending in the LRO phase (both finite-temperature and zero-temperature) follow conventional power-law scaling without logarithmic corrections.
AI.conclusion: The results clearly uncover the characteristic scaling corrections of the J1-J2 Potts model and offer theoretical guidance for future experimental investigations of KZM via photonic simulation platforms.

title: Exact static exchange benchmark for the uniform electron gas: Dynamic-kernel tests and exchange-correlation cancellation near 2kF
summary: The static local field factors of the uniform electron gas are known accurately from quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) calculations, but two of their most striking features have lacked a mechanism: $G_+$ grows almost exactly as $q^2$ up to nearly $2k_F$, and the violent $2k_F$ physics of the Fermi surface leaves only a faint trace in it. Combining the textbook first-order local-field relation with the exact static exchange polarizability gives a compact exact benchmark: the universal exchange-only local field factor $G_x(q,0) = -I(Q)Q^2/L(Q)^2$, $Q = q/2k_F$, with exact values $(1/4)(q/k_F)^2$ at small $q$, $π^2/6$ at $2k_F$ -- apparently never before stated as a local-field value -- and $1/3$ at large $q$, giving the exchange-only spin-averaged contact value $g(0) = 1/2$ of the unpolarized gas (BDL 1977). $G_x$ rises to a finite maximum of 1.9924 at $1.9685k_F$ and passes through $π^2/6$ at exactly $2k_F$ with a slope diverging as $\ln^3|q-2k_F|$. Against this benchmark, the 1980 BDL tabulation is accurate to about one percent below $1.5k_F$, while the 2024 McLachlan-variational kernel of Nazarov and Silkin is two-percent accurate only below $0.5k_F$, is a factor of 1.74 low at $2k_F$, and its large-q limit is inconsistent with the contact constraint. A spin-resolved decomposition of QMC local field factors about the exact baseline shows that, within the resolution and smoothness assumptions of the QMC-based representations, both features follow from a strong exchange-correlation cancellation: at the QMC point closest to $2k_F$ ($q = 2.01k_F$, $r_s = 2$), correlation cancels 0.43(7) of the exact exchange value 1.33. Computed consistently at each wavevector, the static exchange-kernel thresholds derived from the closed form reproduce, to 0.2%, the finite-wavevector charge threshold $r_s \approx 10.6$ near $q = 1.94k_F$ obtained numerically in 1980, and recovered again in 2014.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an exact closed-form expression for the exchange-only local field factor $G_x(q,0)$ of the uniform electron gas, showing it grows as $q^2$ up to nearly $2k_F$ with a divergent slope at $2k_F$, and uses this benchmark to show that QMC-based local field factors exhibit strong exchange-correlation cancellation near $2k_F$, explaining why the Fermi surface singularity leaves only a faint trace.
AI.motivation: To understand why the static local field factor $G_+$ grows almost exactly as $q^2$ up to $2k_F$ and why the $2k_F$ Fermi surface singularity leaves only a faint trace—two features known from QMC but lacking mechanistic explanation.
AI.method: Combining the textbook first-order local-field relation with the exact static exchange polarizability yields a closed-form exchange-only local field factor $G_x(q,0) = -I(Q)Q^2/L(Q)^2$ with $Q=q/2k_F$. This benchmark is compared against QMC data and existing approximations (BDL 1980, Nazarov-Silkin 2024).
AI.result: The exact $G_x$ grows as $(1/4)(q/k_F)^2$ at small $q$, reaches $\pi^2/6$ at $2k_F$, and $1/3$ at large $q$. Its slope diverges as $\ln^3|q-2k_F|$ at $2k_F$. Correlation cancels 0.43(7) of the exact exchange value 1.33 at the QMC point nearest $2k_F$, explaining the faint $2k_F$ signature.
AI.conclusion: The exact exchange-only local field factor provides a definitive benchmark; the two puzzling features of QMC $G_+$ arise from near-perfect cancellation between exchange and correlation at $2k_F$. The closed form reproduces the charge threshold $r_s \approx 10.6$ near $q=1.94k_F$ to 0.2% accuracy.

title: Reconstructing local environments from concise atomistic representations
summary: Symmetry-based representations of local atomic structure, such as the power spectrum or bispectrum, are routinely used to characterize the structural diversity of datasets and as input features for atomistic machine learning. Although these descriptors systematically incorporate increasingly complex geometric correlations, it remains unclear if a given feature can be mapped back to a discrete point cloud, whether such a reconstruction is unique, and how changes in the descriptor are reflected in the underlying atomic geometry. The choice and discretization of the radial and angular bases, as well as the high dimensionality of the resulting feature vectors -- which may contain hundreds or thousands of components -- make this interpretation even more challenging. In this work, we investigate the inverse problem of recovering atomic structures from invariant descriptors. We show that accurate reconstructions can be obtained from remarkably compact descriptors of different correlation orders, each comprising only a few tens of features. Even representations that are formally incomplete or locally ill-conditioned can be inverted to accurate geometric reconstructions of atomic environments across molecular and material datasets. Our reconstruction framework provides a general algorithmic means of identifying approximate degeneracies of invariant descriptors and recovering distinct atomic environments that cannot be distinguished by a given representation. Finally, by reconstructing atomic configurations from descriptors, we examine how perturbations in invariant descriptors of different correlation orders translate into structural distortions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the inverse problem of reconstructing atomic structures from symmetry-based invariant descriptors (e.g., power spectrum, bispectrum). The authors demonstrate that accurate 3D atomic configurations can be recovered from compact descriptor vectors with only tens of features, even when the descriptors are formally incomplete or ill-conditioned. The framework also identifies degenerate descriptors (distinct structures yielding the same representation) and maps descriptor perturbations to structural distortions.
AI.motivation: Although symmetry-adapted descriptors like the power spectrum and bispectrum are widely used in atomistic machine learning, it is unclear whether these features can be uniquely inverted to recover the original atomic geometry. The high dimensionality, choice of basis functions, and discretization further complicate interpretability. This work aims to solve the inverse mapping problem to improve descriptor interpretability and identify representation degeneracies.
AI.method: The authors develop a reconstruction framework that inverts invariant descriptors of atomic environments back to point cloud geometries. They test compact descriptor sets with only tens of features across different correlation orders, and assess reconstruction accuracy on molecular and material datasets. The framework also identifies approximate degeneracies and analyzes how perturbations in descriptor space translate to structural changes.
AI.result: Accurate atomic structure reconstructions are achieved from remarkably compact descriptors (tens of features). Even formally incomplete or locally ill-conditioned representations can be inverted to high-quality geometries. The framework successfully identifies degenerate descriptor pairs and quantifies how descriptor perturbations map to structural distortions across correlation orders.
AI.conclusion: Invariant descriptors of local atomic environments, despite being high-dimensional and potentially incomplete, can be reliably inverted to recover atomic structures using compact feature sets. This approach provides a general algorithmic tool for interpreting descriptor representations, identifying degeneracies, and linking descriptor space changes to geometric distortions.

title: Coupled-channel approach to scattering of hybrid excitons
summary: We consider the interactions of hybrid excitons in a two-dimensional semiconductor bilayer, where spatially direct and indirect excitons are hybridized by interlayer charge-carrier tunneling. Starting from a microscopic electron-hole description, we construct realistic pseudopotentials for exciton-exciton interactions and use them as inputs to a coupled-channel scattering integral equation. This enables non-perturbative calculations of hybrid-exciton scattering beyond standard perturbative theories, and highlights the importance of energy-dependent scattering and channel mixing. In particular, we show that the interaction strength of hybrid excitons exhibits a rapid growth with increasing energy, which we find is inherited from their indirect-exciton component. We further demonstrate that dielectric screening affects the direct and indirect channels in distinct ways, leading to markedly different interaction strengths across experimentally relevant dielectric environments. Finally, we show that the hybrid-exciton scattering strength can be electrically tuned via the Stark shift, which controls the direct-indirect detuning and hence the hybridization of the two exciton modes.

AI.tldr: Hybrid excitons in 2D semiconductor bilayers are studied using non-perturbative scattering calculations, revealing energy-dependent interaction growth, channel-specific dielectric screening effects, and electrical tunability via Stark shift.
AI.motivation: To understand the interactions of hybrid excitons (mixtures of direct and indirect excitons coupled via interlayer tunneling) beyond standard perturbative theories, particularly their scattering properties and tunability.
AI.method: Microscopic electron-hole description → realistic pseudopotentials for exciton-exciton interactions → coupled-channel scattering integral equation for non-perturbative calculations.
AI.result: (1) Hybrid-exciton interaction strength grows rapidly with energy, inherited from indirect-exciton component. (2) Dielectric screening affects direct and indirect channels differently. (3) Scattering strength is electrically tunable via Stark shift controlling direct-indirect detuning and hybridization.
AI.conclusion: Non-perturbative methods reveal important energy-dependent scattering and channel mixing effects that standard perturbative theories miss, and demonstrate multiple knobs (energy, dielectric environment, electric field) for controlling hybrid-exciton interactions.

title: A Thermodynamic Pinning Criterion for Two-Dimensional Structural Superlubricity
summary: Incommensurability and elastic reconstruction do not by themselves define a structurally superlubric phase. We define fully sliding and pinned zero-temperature phases by $\limsup_{A\to\infty}τ_{\rm dep}^{\max}(A)=0$ and $\liminf_{A\to\infty}τ_{\rm dep}^{\min}(A)>0$, respectively; $Λ_n=|V_n|G_{n,i}[D_{\rm rel}^{-1}(\mathbf q_n)]_{ij}G_{n,j}$ measures only reconstruction susceptibility. Translational covariance then proves that a clean, smooth, infinite moiré continuum can reconstruct without acquiring a bulk sliding barrier. We restore atomic sampling in a two-dimensional discrete model of graphene/hBN and test both a diffusion quantum Monte Carlo first-star potential and a 15-harmonic Leven potential across three rational approximants and five directions. No physical-coupling equilibrium or metastable barrier is resolved. The Leven spectrum raises the largest tested $Λ$ from $0.142$ to $0.212$, while artificial scaling through $Λ=1$ reaches uncontrolled strain before a size-independent threshold appears. The tested zero-temperature in-plane models are therefore consistent with an elastically relaxed sliding regime; $Λ=1$ is a reconstruction scale, not a static phase criterion.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes rigorous criteria for structurally superlubric phases, showing that incommensurability and elastic reconstruction alone are insufficient. Using translational covariance, it demonstrates that moiré continua can reconstruct without sliding barriers. Atomic-scale models of graphene/hBN (using DMC and Leven potentials) find no physical equilibrium or metastable barriers, and Λ=1 is identified as a reconstruction scale rather than a phase transition criterion.
AI.motivation: To resolve whether incommensurability and elastic reconstruction define structural superlubricity, the authors seek rigorous thermodynamic-limit criteria for pinned vs. fully sliding phases and test whether reconstructed moiré interfaces inherently acquire sliding barriers.
AI.method: Rigorous zero-temperature phase definitions using limsup/liminf of depinning thresholds; translational covariance analysis of moiré continua; discrete 2D modeling of graphene/hBN with diffusion quantum Monte Carlo and Leven interlayer potentials across three rational approximants and five sliding directions.
AI.result: No physical-coupling equilibrium or metastable sliding barriers were resolved. The Leven potential's largest Λ rose from 0.142 to 0.212; artificial scaling to Λ=1 produced uncontrolled strain without a size-independent threshold. Clean moiré continua can reconstruct without a bulk sliding barrier.
AI.conclusion: The zero-temperature in-plane models are consistent with an elastically relaxed sliding regime. Λ=1 is a reconstruction scale, not a static phase criterion—reconstruction does not necessarily imply pinning.

title: Multi-Criticality and RG Topology in the Charge-Kondo-Breakdown Scenario in the Cuprates
summary: In this paper, we examine the dynamical charge-Kondo-breakdown scenario proposed for cuprate superconductors within the perspective of renormalization group (RG) topology. By analyzing the coupled RG flow equations governing the effective low-energy theory, we determine the fixed-point structure, stability properties, and global organization of the flow. We find that the putative finite-coupling interacting fixed point is unstable against perturbations transverse to an invariant critical manifold. As a result, generic RG trajectories exhibit runaway behavior. To elucidate the global structure of the theory, we combine analytical solutions of the flow equations with numerical phase portraits and Poincaré compactification. This analysis reveals that the interacting fixed point exhibits a marginally relevant instability, generating an exponentially large but finite crossover scale. The resulting flow topology closely resembles anisotropy-driven runaway flows encountered in fluctuation-induced weakly first-order transitions. Within this framework, the apparent quantum-critical regime can be understood as an extended crossover controlled by a near-critical fixed point, rather than by asymptotic scale invariance. The results obtained indicate that the existence of extended scaling behavior does not, by itself, imply the presence of a stable interacting quantum critical state. More generally, our analysis demonstrates how RG topology can provide a powerful diagnostic for distinguishing genuine criticality from pseudo-critical behavior in theories of strongly correlated quantum matter.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the charge-Kondo-breakdown scenario in cuprates using RG topology, finding that the interacting fixed point is unstable, leading to runaway flow and a finite crossover scale that mimics quantum criticality without true asymptotic scale invariance.
AI.motivation: To critically examine whether the putative quantum critical fixed point in the charge-Kondo-breakdown scenario for cuprate superconductors is truly stable, or whether the observed scaling behavior arises from pseudo-critical crossover dynamics.
AI.method: Renormalization group (RG) analysis of coupled flow equations, including fixed-point stability analysis, analytical solutions, numerical phase portraits, and Poincaré compactification to study global flow topology.
AI.result: The interacting fixed point is unstable against transverse perturbations, yielding runaway RG trajectories. The instability is marginally relevant, generating an exponentially large but finite crossover scale. The flow topology resembles anisotropy-driven fluctuation-induced weakly first-order transitions.
AI.conclusion: Extended scaling behavior does not necessarily imply a stable interacting quantum critical state; RG topology is a powerful tool for distinguishing genuine criticality from pseudo-critical behavior in strongly correlated systems.

title: Rem3Di: Learning smooth, chiral 3D molecular descriptors from atomistic foundation models
comment: An earlier version of this work appeared at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps). Workshop version: https://openreview.net/forum?id=jOmZsvXoK5
summary: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on large quantum-mechanical datasets and generalise across broad regions of chemical and configurational space. Beyond their usual role in accelerating sampling-based simulations, their internal representations encode chemically rich local atomic environments. Here, we introduce Rem3Di, a representation-learning framework that repurposes latent features from atomistic foundation models as transferable molecular descriptors for property prediction and virtual screening. Rem3Di combines a potential's per-atom features into a single fixed-length descriptor of the whole molecule that varies smoothly with three-dimensional structure and is invariant to the ordering of the atoms. The descriptor can be used directly or fine-tuned for specific prediction tasks. To capture molecular handedness, Rem3Di constructs pseudoscalar features, which are unchanged by rotation but reverse sign under mirror reflection. This lets the descriptor distinguish enantiomers, which can differ in activity and toxicity. The transformer is pretrained on large molecular datasets by reconstructing corrupted atom features, so no experimental labels are required. Across public drug-property benchmarks, Rem3Di matches or exceeds published baselines without relying on classical 2D fingerprints. Additionally, the same descriptor yields chemically meaningful differentiation of transition-metal complexes without predefined bonding rules or handcrafted representations. Rem3Di therefore provides a route from simulation-trained atomistic representations to transferable, chirality-aware molecular representations for chemical machine learning.

AI.tldr: Rem3Di repurposes latent features from foundation MLIPs as transferable, chirality-aware molecular descriptors for property prediction and virtual screening, matching or exceeding baselines across drug-property benchmarks and transition-metal complexes without needing 2D fingerprints or handcrafted rules.
AI.motivation: To leverage internal representations of foundation MLIPs—trained on large quantum-mechanical datasets—as transferable molecular descriptors for property prediction and virtual screening, overcoming limitations of classical 2D fingerprints and handcrafted representations.
AI.method: Rem3Di combines per-atom features from a foundation MLIP into a fixed-length, smooth, permutation-invariant molecular descriptor. It constructs pseudoscalar features (rotation-invariant, sign-reversing under mirror reflection) to capture chirality. The descriptor can be used directly or fine-tuned; the transformer is pretrained via reconstructing corrupted atom features without requiring experimental labels.
AI.result: On public drug-property benchmarks, Rem3Di matches or exceeds published baselines without classical 2D fingerprints. It also yields chemically meaningful differentiation of transition-metal complexes without predefined bonding rules or handcrafted representations.
AI.conclusion: Rem3Di provides a route from simulation-trained atomistic representations to transferable, chirality-aware molecular representations for chemical machine learning, enabling broad applications in property prediction and virtual screening.

title: Derivation of the Boltzmann equation with no "molecular chaos"-type approximation
summary: The paper resolves the problem of the derivation of a completely closed evolution equation for $s$-particle distribution function $F_s(t)$ ($s \le N$) from the Liouville equation for $N \gg 1$-particle distribution function $F_N(t)$ with arbitrary initial condition $F_N(0)$ and without any use of the "molecular chaos" type approximation. The initial correlations are accounted for in this equation in the kernel governing the evolution of $F_s(t)$ via the special projection operator which exactly transforms the inhomogeneous Nakajima-Zwanzig Generalized Master Equation (GME) with an irrelevant initial condition term into the homogenous one. This equation is further simplified by presenting its kernel in the linear in the particles' density $n$ approximation. In this approximation the equations for one-particle $F_1(t)$ and two-particle $F_2(t)$ distribution functions are derived. It is shown that the terms describing the influence of initial correlations in the equation for $F_1(t)$ disappear at the large timescale $t \sim t_{\text{rel}} \gg t_{\text{cor}}$ ($t_{\text{cor}}$ is a short correlation time as compared to a relaxation time $t_{\text{rel}}$ of $F_1(t)$) resulting in the linear Boltzmann equation. This equation can be presented as the nonlinear Boltzmann equation in the time interval $t_{\text{cor}} \ll t \ll t_{\text{rel}}$. At $t_{\text{rel}} \to \infty$ (mean free path $l \to \infty$) the Boltzmann equation holds for all finite times $t \gg t_{\text{cor}}$.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a closed evolution equation for the s-particle distribution function from the Liouville equation without using molecular chaos approximations, accounting for initial correlations via a projection operator. In the low-density approximation, the one-particle equation reduces to the linear Boltzmann equation at large timescales and to the nonlinear Boltzmann equation at intermediate timescales.
AI.motivation: To derive a closed evolution equation for the s-particle distribution function from first principles (Liouville equation) without relying on the "molecular chaos" approximation, and to properly account for initial correlations in the kinetic description.
AI.method: The authors transform the inhomogeneous Nakajima-Zwanzig Generalized Master Equation (GME) into a homogeneous one using a special projection operator that accounts for initial correlations. The resulting kernel is then simplified in the linear density approximation to derive equations for one- and two-particle distribution functions.
AI.result: In the linear density approximation, terms describing initial correlations in the equation for F_1(t) vanish at large timescales (t ~ t_rel ≫ t_cor), yielding the linear Boltzmann equation. At intermediate timescales (t_cor ≪ t ≪ t_rel), it reduces to the nonlinear Boltzmann equation. When t_rel → ∞ (mean free path l → ∞), the Boltzmann equation holds for all finite times t ≫ t_cor.
AI.conclusion: A rigorous derivation of the Boltzmann equation from the Liouville equation is achieved without molecular chaos assumptions, with explicit treatment of initial correlations that are shown to become irrelevant at relaxation timescales.

title: Majorana bound states in anisotropic and tilted Dirac and Weyl systems
summary: Topological superconductors host Majorana boundary modes whose robustness is protected by the nontrivial topology of the bulk Bogoliubov quasiparticle spectrum. While Majorana bound states associated with Dirac and Weyl quasiparticles have been extensively investigated, much less is known about how anisotropic quasiparticle velocities and tilted band structures modify their microscopic properties. Here, we develop an analytical framework for Majorana bound states in effective two-dimensional (2D) Bogoliubov--de Gennes Dirac theories describing the surface quasiparticles of topological superconductors and extend the analysis to three-dimensional (3D) tilted Weyl systems by establishing a microscopic connection to the same low-energy description through superconducting pairing. For anisotropic 2D Dirac systems, we derive closed analytical expressions for the continuum topological invariant, Majorana wave function, localization length, propagation velocity, and finite-size minigap for arbitrary interface orientations. We show that the chirality of the Majorana channel is determined by the sign of the velocity-matrix determinant, while its localization and dispersion are governed jointly by the velocity tensor and the interface geometry. For tilted 2D Dirac cones, we demonstrate that the tilt leaves the spinor eigenstates, Berry phase, and projected pairing symmetry unchanged, but strongly suppresses the Majorana propagation velocity and finite-size minigap as the Lifshitz transition between type-I and type-II regimes is approached. Finally, we consider superconducting tilted 3D Weyl systems and show that the projection of a conventional spin-singlet $s$-wave pairing interaction onto the low-energy Weyl bands naturally generates an effective chiral $p_x\pm ip_y$ pairing symmetry, providing a microscopic Bogoliubov--de Gennes description that supports localized Majorana surface states.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an analytical framework for Majorana bound states in 2D and 3D topological superconductors, focusing on how anisotropic quasiparticle velocities and tilted band structures affect their properties. It derives closed-form expressions for key quantities in anisotropic 2D Dirac systems, shows tilt suppresses Majorana velocity and minigap near the Lifshitz transition, and demonstrates that s-wave pairing in tilted 3D Weyl systems generates effective chiral p±ip pairing supporting Majorana surface states.
AI.motivation: While Majorana bound states in Dirac and Weyl systems have been extensively studied, the effects of anisotropic quasiparticle velocities and tilted band structures on their microscopic properties remain poorly understood. This paper aims to fill that gap.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytical framework based on effective 2D Bogoliubov-de Gennes Dirac theories for surface quasiparticles of topological superconductors, extended to 3D tilted Weyl systems via microscopic connection through superconducting pairing. They derive closed analytical expressions for topological invariants, wave functions, localization lengths, propagation velocities, and finite-size minigaps.
AI.result: The chirality of the Majorana channel is determined by the sign of the velocity-matrix determinant. Localization and dispersion depend jointly on the velocity tensor and interface geometry. Tilt leaves spinor eigenstates, Berry phase, and projected pairing unchanged but strongly suppresses Majorana velocity and minigap near the type-I/type-II Lifshitz transition. In 3D tilted Weyl systems, s-wave pairing generates effective chiral p±ip pairing.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropy and tilt significantly modify Majorana bound state properties, with implications for their robustness and experimental detection. The work provides a unified low-energy description linking 2D and 3D topological superconductors with anisotropic band structures.

title: Numerical exploration on unveiling the photovoltaic potential of MgXS3(X = Ti, Zr, Hf) chalcogenide perovskites
summary: Lead-free chalcogenide perovskites offer a nontoxic and thermally robust path beyond Pb-based perovskite solar cells (PSCs), but their device-level behavior in realistic three-dimensional geometries remains insufficiently characterized. In this work, we investigate ZnSe/MgXS3(X = Ti, Zr, Hf)/Sb2S3 solar cell architecture where MgXS3 absorbers from the II-IV-VI chalcogenide perovskite family is employed as the absorber layer. The device is analyzed using 3D finite-element simulations in COMSOL Multiphysics that self-consistently couple optical generation, drift-diffusion carrier transport, and heat transfer under AM 1.5G 1-sun illumination, following a fully coupled opto-electro-thermal framework. For each absorber composition, the impacts of absorber thickness, doping, and defect density are systematically investigated, and the contribution of an Sb2S3 back-surface-field (BSF) layer to carrier collection and spectral response is quantified. Under optimized conditions, MgZrS3, MgTiS3, MgHfS3-based devices achieves a simulated power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 28.18%, 26.72%, and 28.16%, respectively. The corresponding open-circuit voltage (VOC) values are 0.94 V, 0.74 V, and, 1.07 V while the short-circuit current density (JSC) values are 34.46 mA/cm2, 42.69 mA/cm2, and 29.89 mA/cm2, with fill factor (FF) values of 86.99%, 84.58%, and 88.02%, respectively. Coupled electro-thermal simulations further reveal a small spatially non-uniform steady-state temperature rise across the ultrathin cell stack, mainly governed by non-radiative recombination and Joule dissipation within the active layers. Overall, these results confirm MgXS3(X = Ti, Zr, Hf) chalcogenide perovskites as promising lead-free absorber materials and offer practical design guidance for achieving high-efficiency, thermally stable three-dimensional device architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper uses 3D opto-electro-thermal simulations to analyze lead-free chalcogenide perovskite solar cells with ZnSe/MgXS₃(X=Ti, Zr, Hf)/Sb₂S₃ architecture, achieving high PCEs of up to 28.18% while confirming thermal stability and non-toxic viability.
AI.motivation: Lead-free chalcogenide perovskites offer nontoxic and thermally robust alternatives to Pb-based perovskite solar cells, but their device-level behavior in realistic 3D geometries remains insufficiently characterized.
AI.method: 3D finite-element simulations in COMSOL Multiphysics using a fully coupled opto-electro-thermal framework under AM 1.5G 1-sun illumination, analyzing absorber thickness, doping, defect density, and Sb₂S₃ back-surface-field (BSF) layer contributions.
AI.result: MgZrS₃ achieves PCE=28.18% (VOC=0.94V, JSC=34.46mA/cm², FF=86.99%), MgTiS₃ achieves PCE=26.72% (VOC=0.74V, JSC=42.69mA/cm², FF=84.58%), MgHfS₃ achieves PCE=28.16% (VOC=1.07V, JSC=29.89mA/cm², FF=88.02%). Small non-uniform temperature rise primarily from non-radiative recombination and Joule dissipation.
AI.conclusion: MgXS₃ (X=Ti, Zr, Hf) chalcogenide perovskites are promising lead-free absorber materials, providing practical design guidance for high-efficiency, thermally stable 3D device architectures.

title: Spatially Dispersive Second-Harmonic Generation in Ferroaxial Systems
summary: Spatially dispersive second-harmonic generation (SHG) provides a powerful probe of centrosymmetric multipolar states beyond the electric-dipole approximation. We develop a gauge-consistent microscopic theory of spatially dispersive SHG that treats electric-quadrupole (EQ) and magnetic-dipole (MD) processes on equal footing. Applying the formulation to a minimal triangular cluster model with ferroaxial order, which is closely related to an electric toroidal dipole, we show that the nonlinear optical response directly reflects the ferroaxial order parameter. The agreement between length- and velocity-gauge calculations confirms the gauge consistency of the formulation. We further demonstrate that the EQ and MD contributions exhibit different spectral weights despite sharing the same resonance energies. In particular, the MD channel can dominate over the EQ channel at selected resonances, indicating that it is not merely a perturbative correction. Our results establish that both EQ and MD processes are essential for a quantitative description of spatially dispersive SHG in ferroaxial materials and provide a microscopic basis for interpreting nonlinear optical signatures of centrosymmetric multipolar order.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a gauge-consistent microscopic theory of spatially dispersive second-harmonic generation (SHG) treating electric-quadrupole (EQ) and magnetic-dipole (MD) processes equally. Applied to a ferroaxial triangular cluster model, it shows SHG reflects ferroaxial order, with EQ and MD contributions having different spectral weights and MD potentially dominating at certain resonances, establishing both processes as essential for quantitative SHG descriptions in ferroaxial materials.
AI.motivation: To develop a gauge-consistent microscopic theory of spatially dispersive SHG that treats EQ and MD processes on equal footing, providing a microscopic basis for interpreting nonlinear optical signatures of centrosymmetric multipolar order, particularly in ferroaxial materials.
AI.method: Gauge-consistent microscopic formulation of spatially dispersive SHG incorporating both EQ and MD contributions; applied to a minimal triangular cluster model with ferroaxial order (related to electric toroidal dipole); length- and velocity-gauge calculations compared to verify consistency.
AI.result: The nonlinear optical response directly reflects the ferroaxial order parameter. EQ and MD contributions share the same resonance energies but exhibit different spectral weights. The MD channel can dominate over the EQ channel at selected resonances, showing it is not merely a perturbative correction.
AI.conclusion: Both EQ and MD processes are essential for a quantitative description of spatially dispersive SHG in ferroaxial materials. The work provides a microscopic foundation for interpreting nonlinear optical signatures of centrosymmetric multipolar order.

title: Investigating aqueous mineral interfaces using sum frequency generation spectroscopy
summary: Sum frequency generation spectroscopy can be utilized to address the challenge of studying solid-liquid interfaces under ambient pressure and with macroscopic amounts of liquid, while still retrieving molecular level information. By utilizing a non-linear optical process, this method allows to selectively measure vibrations of interfacial species. Within this chapter sum frequency generation spectroscopy is first briefly introduced and then comprehensively evaluated as an investigative tool for solid-liquid interfaces, with mineral-water interfaces as model system. Additionally, it is explained how the actual probing depth of this method depends on both the experimental setup and the properties of the investigated system, such as surface charges.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses how sum frequency generation (SFG) spectroscopy can be used to study solid-liquid interfaces at ambient pressure, with mineral-water interfaces as a model system. It explains the method's selectivity for interfacial vibrations, its probing depth dependency on experimental setup and system properties like surface charges.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of studying solid-liquid interfaces under ambient pressure with macroscopic liquid amounts while still obtaining molecular-level information.
AI.method: Sum frequency generation (SFG) spectroscopy, a non-linear optical technique that selectively measures vibrations of interfacial species.
AI.result: SFG spectroscopy enables molecular-level investigation of solid-liquid interfaces at ambient pressure. The probing depth depends on both the experimental setup and system properties such as surface charges.
AI.conclusion: SFG spectroscopy is a valuable tool for investigating solid-liquid interfaces, with its probing depth being tunable and dependent on experimental and system-specific parameters.

title: Random walks in Dirichlet random environment in dimension $d+1$
comment: 27 pages, 13 figures. Data gnuplot files for plots available at https://dare.uol.de/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.57782/G0HPXH
summary: The atypical behaviour of random walks in time-dependent random environment was recently related to Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) growth. While this is now well-understood in spatial dimension $d=1$, further efforts are necessary to better understand these connections in dimensions $d>1$. In this paper, we study this problem numerically for $d=1, 2$ and $3$, focusing on a discrete model with Dirichlet distributed transition probabilities. This model is a generalization of an integrable model in $d=1$, and it has the advantage of admitting an explicit, product-form, stationary measure. We verify that the growth of the variance of the logarithm of point-to-point probabilities, namely from the origin to position $x$ in time $t$, is compatible with KPZ growth in dimension $d=1$ and $d=2$. In spatial dimension $d=3$, we confirm the existence of a phase transition as the angle $\vert x\vert /t$ increases and we obtain a lower bound based on an exact second moment calculation. We find that in the weak disorder phase the point-to-point probability acquires a heavy tailed distribution, and that in the strong disorder phase the cumulants of its logarithm grow with time. Further, we show that for this model, we can compute exactly the sample to sample variance of the thermal average $\overline{ \langle x \rangle^2}$ and that it is related to the extreme diffusion coefficient introduced recently.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically studies random walks in time-dependent random environments for d=1,2,3 using a discrete model with Dirichlet-distributed transition probabilities, finding KPZ growth compatibility in d=1 and d=2, a phase transition in d=3, and connections to extreme diffusion coefficients.
AI.motivation: While the connection between random walks in time-dependent random environments and KPZ growth is well-understood in d=1, further understanding is needed for dimensions d>1.
AI.method: Numerical study for d=1,2,3 using a discrete model with Dirichlet distributed transition probabilities, a generalization of an integrable model in d=1 with explicit product-form stationary measure.
AI.result: KPZ-compatible growth in d=1 and d=2; phase transition in d=3 as |x|/t increases; weak disorder phase has heavy-tailed distributions; strong disorder phase shows growing cumulants; exact expression for sample-to-sample variance of thermal average relates to extreme diffusion coefficient.
AI.conclusion: The model extends KPZ connections to higher dimensions, reveals a phase transition in d=3, and provides exact results for variance and diffusion coefficients.

title: Nonreciprocal phonon propagation via spatially asymmetric magnon-phonon coupling
summary: Nonreciprocal propagation of surface acoustic waves (SAWs) based on the spatial asymmetry of magnon-phonon coupling is demonstrated. This nonreciprocity is enabled by an acoustic wavelength scale thick magnetic layer formed under a thin piezoelectric film. In this configuration, magnon modes activated by dipole-dipole interactions are localized near either the top or bottom interface depending on the propagation direction of the SAW. As a result, the spatial overlap between interfacial magnon and surface phonon modes is expected to become direction dependent, in a manner that leads to distinct unidirectional propagation of SAWs. Notably, the resulting nonreciprocity reaches the highest level among those reported for SAW devices based on a single magnetic layer. This finding will establish a new strategy of nonreciprocal acoustic propagation in a structurally simple magnomechanical device.

AI.tldr: A new mechanism for nonreciprocal surface acoustic wave propagation is demonstrated using spatial asymmetry of magnon-phonon coupling in a structure with a thick magnetic layer under a thin piezoelectric film. The nonreciprocity arises from direction-dependent spatial overlap between interfacial magnon modes and surface phonon modes, achieving the highest reported level for a single magnetic layer SAW device.
AI.motivation: To achieve nonreciprocal SAW propagation using a structurally simple single-magnetic-layer configuration, avoiding complex multi-layer designs while maximizing nonreciprocity.
AI.method: A thick magnetic layer is formed under a thin piezoelectric film. Dipole-dipole interactions activate magnon modes localized near either the top or bottom interface depending on SAW propagation direction, creating direction-dependent spatial overlap between interfacial magnon and surface phonon modes.
AI.result: The nonreciprocity achieved is the highest level reported for SAW devices based on a single magnetic layer.
AI.conclusion: This establishes a new strategy for nonreciprocal acoustic propagation in a structurally simple magnomechanical device.

title: The origin of ferroelectricity, polarization and high resistivity in Aurivillius CaBi2B2O9 (B = Ta, Nb)
summary: Aurivillius layered oxides are important candidates for high-temperature ferroelectric and piezoelectric application. In this work, we combine group theoretic analysis with first-principles calculations to systematically investigate the origin of ferroelectric phase transition, polarization, piezoelectric response, and intrinsic electrical insulation of the two-layer Aurivillius ferroelectrics CaBi$_{2}$B$_{2}$O$_{9}$ (B = Ta, Nb). The results show that the \textit{A2$_1$am} ferroelectric phase arises from the cooperative condensation of a polar mode and nonpolar oxygen octahedral rotation/tilting modes, whose the $Γ_5^-$X$_2^+$X$_3^-$ trilinear coupling substantially lowers the total energy and deepens the ferroelectric potential well. The spontaneous polarization and anisotropic piezoelectric response are governed primarily by the cooperative displacements of the Bi$_{2}$O$_{2}$ layers and Ta/NbO$_{6}$ octahedra, with Bi ions providing an indispensable contribution to both responses. More importantly, the polar distortion can be traced to the relative in-plane displacement between adjacent the Bi$_{2}$O$_{2}$ layer and the perovskite-like block. Because this displacement is intrinsic to the alternating Bi$_{2}$O$_{2}$/perovskite-block stacking topology and is independent of the number of perovskite layers, we identify interlayer sliding as a general, layer-number-independent structural mechanism for ferroelectricity in Aurivillius oxides. Our findings establish a unified microscopic picture linking structural distortions, ferroelectric polarization, piezoelectric response, and electronic insulation in CaBi$_{2}$B$_{2}$O$_{9}$ (B = Ta, Nb), and provide theoretical guidance for designing layered ferroelectric oxides with high Curie temperatures and robust insulating behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper uses group theory and first-principles calculations to investigate the origin of ferroelectricity in Aurivillius oxides CaBi₂B₂O₉ (B=Ta, Nb), identifying interlayer sliding between Bi₂O₂ layers and perovskite blocks as a general, layer-number-independent mechanism for ferroelectricity, governed by Γ₅⁻-X₂⁺-X₃⁻ trilinear coupling.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental origin of ferroelectric phase transitions, polarization, piezoelectric response, and electrical insulation in two-layer Aurivillius ferroelectrics, and to establish a unified microscopic picture linking these properties.
AI.method: Combined group theoretic analysis and first-principles density functional theory calculations to systematically study the structural distortions, mode condensation, and coupling mechanisms in CaBi₂B₂O₉ (B=Ta, Nb).
AI.result: The A2₁am ferroelectric phase arises from cooperative condensation of a polar mode and nonpolar oxygen octahedral rotation/tilting modes via Γ₅⁻-X₂⁺-X₃⁻ trilinear coupling. Polarization and piezoelectric response are governed by cooperative displacements of Bi₂O₂ layers and Ta/NbO₆ octahedra. The polar distortion originates from relative in-plane displacement between adjacent Bi₂O₂ layer and perovskite-like block, identifying interlayer sliding as a general, layer-number-independent mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a unified microscopic picture linking structural distortions, ferroelectric polarization, piezoelectric response, and electronic insulation in CaBi₂B₂O₉, providing theoretical guidance for designing layered ferroelectric oxides with high Curie temperatures and robust insulating behavior.

title: How to measure loop currents in scanning tunneling microscopy
summary: The emergence of loop current phases, where spontaneous loops of orbital currents give rise to a weak local magnetic moments, has been proposed to exist in a number of quantum materials based on measurements that pick up weak signatures of time reversal symmetry breaking or small magnetic moment order. The most prominent example is as an explanation of the pseudogap phase on the underdoped side of the phase diagram of the high-temperature cuprate superconductors, but more recently, it has been proposed to occur in Kagome materials and at the surface layer of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$. Experimental results have, however, been inconclusive so far, some detecting signatures that can be understood as emerging due to loop current phases, whilst others have not detected any significant proof. One of the techniques that should be able to pick up local signatures of loop current orders is low temperature scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS), however firm predictions of how to detect them are missing. Here, we provide specific predictions for how loop current orders in a square lattice can be seen in spectroscopic maps, using models of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors and of the surface layer of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$. We find that, besides lifting degeneracies at the specific ordering vector of the loop current order, a finite spin polarisation emerges when spin-orbit coupling is present, signatures of which can be detected in spin-polarised STM.

AI.tldr: This paper predicts specific spectroscopic signatures of loop current orders in square lattice materials (cuprates and Sr₂RuO₄) detectable via STM/STS, including degeneracy lifting at the ordering vector and spin-polarized signals when spin-orbit coupling is present.
AI.motivation: Loop current phases have been proposed to exist in several quantum materials (cuprates, Kagome materials, Sr₂RuO₄), but experimental detection has been inconclusive. STM/STS should be able to detect them, but firm predictions for how to identify loop current orders in spectroscopic maps have been missing.
AI.method: The authors use models of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors and the surface layer of Sr₂RuO₄ to compute spectroscopic signatures of loop current orders in a square lattice, examining both the lifting of degeneracies at the ordering vector and the emergence of finite spin polarization under spin-orbit coupling.
AI.result: Loop current orders lift degeneracies at the specific ordering vector, and when spin-orbit coupling is present, a finite spin polarization emerges that can be detected via spin-polarized STM.
AI.conclusion: The work provides specific, actionable predictions for detecting loop current orders using STM/STS, offering a path to resolve the long-standing experimental ambiguity surrounding these phases in cuprates, Sr₂RuO₄, and related materials.

title: A Comprehensive Experimental and Theoretical Spectroscopic Study of Proteinogenic Amino Acids
summary: Amino acids are essential building blocks of life, yet our understanding of their chemistry and electronic structure in the solid state remains limited. This is particularly important because amino acids in the solid state are relevant to biological and pharmaceutical processes. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy provides a powerful experimental probe of chemical states and occupied electronic structure; however, most spectroscopy studies of amino acids focus on gas-phase species or surface adsorbates, while crystalline amino acids remain underexplored, largely because of experimental challenges associated with radiation damage. Additionally, the spectra are often complex and difficult to interpret, motivating a combined experimental-theoretical approach. This study combines X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations to systematically investigate the core, semi-core, and valence states of 20 proteinogenic amino acids as well as selenomethionine which can be incorporated during protein synthesis and deliver the essential nutrient, Se, required by humans. Calculated relative core binding energies show excellent agreement with experiment and enable reliable assignments. Projections of the density of states provide insight into the influence of local coordination and extended crystal structure, yielding a systematic understanding of the electronic structure and bonding in solid-state AAs. The insights gained from this study enhance the understanding of crystalline amino acids and validate the robustness of an integrated experiment--theory framework.

AI.tldr: This study combines X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and DFT calculations to systematically analyze core, semi-core, and valence states of 20 proteinogenic amino acids and selenomethionine in crystalline form, achieving excellent agreement between experiment and theory and enabling reliable spectral assignments.
AI.motivation: Understanding the electronic structure of crystalline amino acids is important for biological and pharmaceutical processes, but experimental challenges (radiation damage) and spectral complexity have limited prior work to gas-phase or surface-adsorbed species.
AI.method: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy combined with density functional theory (DFT) calculations; systematic investigation of core, semi-core, and valence states; density of states projections to analyze coordination and crystal structure effects.
AI.result: Calculated relative core binding energies agree excellently with experimental values, enabling reliable spectral assignments; density of states projections reveal how local coordination and extended crystal structure influence electronic structure and bonding.
AI.conclusion: The integrated experiment-theory framework provides systematic understanding of electronic structure in solid-state amino acids, overcoming prior experimental limitations and validating the robustness of this combined approach.

title: Optimal Finite-Time Control of Nonreciprocal Brownian Dimers: Thermodynamic Anomaly and Multiple Transitions
summary: We solve exactly a finite-time thermodynamic optimal control problem for two nonreciprocally interacting Brownian particles translated by two harmonic traps. The controller manipulates both the center and separation of the pair. Nonreciprocal interactions generate an internal active force that couples these two channels. The optimal protocol is oscillatory, deliberately opens the dimer even when the target separation is unchanged, and can extract work during transport. A central finding is a finite critical time beyond which the external-work infimum is $-\infty$: at any prescribed duration beyond this threshold, both extractable work and output power are unbounded. Physical regularizations such as finite trap range and force saturation restore a finite optimum and convert the anomaly into optimal-protocol transitions: in the zero-target case, a hard finite range produces a first-order-like jump from the zero protocol to a maximum-range protocol, whereas smooth force saturation gives a continuous, second-order-like onset. Under finite-range constraints, the optimal protocol can further undergo multiple finite-time transitions, producing multiple work-duration kinks with no qualitative analog in prior studies.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically solves optimal control of two nonreciprocally interacting Brownian particles in harmonic traps, finding that beyond a critical finite time, extractable work becomes unbounded; physical regularizations (finite trap range, force saturation) restore finite optima and introduce novel phase transitions in optimal protocols.
AI.motivation: To understand finite-time thermodynamic optimal control in systems with nonreciprocal interactions, which generate internal active forces coupling control channels, and to explore the anomaly of unbounded work extraction at long durations.
AI.method: Exact analytical solution of a finite-time thermodynamic optimal control problem for two nonreciprocally interacting Brownian particles translated by harmonic traps, with both center and separation controlled; regularizations via finite trap range and force saturation are analyzed.
AI.result: Optimal protocol is oscillatory; a finite critical time exists beyond which the external-work infimum is -∞ (unbounded extractable work and power); regularizations restore finite optima, yielding first-order-like (hard cutoff) or second-order-like (smooth saturation) transitions, with multiple finite-time transitions under finite-range constraints.
AI.conclusion: Nonreciprocal interactions enable qualitatively new thermodynamic control phenomena, including unbounded work extraction anomalies and novel optimal-protocol phase transitions, with implications for active matter and information engines.

title: Microscopic Conversion of Structural Chirality into Electronic Chirality in Artificial Chiral Clusters
summary:
We investigate how structural chirality is converted into electronic chirality in a two-dimensional cluster model consisting of a triangular-lattice core and three rod-like extensions under a surface-induced polar field.
  By evaluating the electric toroidal monopole (ETM) and the Edelstein effect, we show that both quantities exhibit antisymmetric and nonmonotonic dependence
  on the structural parameter controlling the cluster geometry.
  While the total density of states is almost unaffected by the structural deformation, the ETM-resolved spectrum changes significantly, indicating that chirality is encoded in the symmetry character of the electronic states rather than in the overall electronic spectrum.
  Real-space analysis reveals that the induced ETM is concentrated near the vertices and rods, whereas the Edelstein response extends more broadly into the core region.
  Furthermore, a parameter-decomposition analysis identifies spin-orbit coupling, surface-induced parity mixing, and structural chirality as the essential ingredients for both phenomena.
  Our results clarify the microscopic connection between structural chirality, electronic chirality, and chiral transport responses in artificial surface nanostructures.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the conversion of structural chirality into electronic chirality in a two-dimensional cluster model (triangular-lattice core with rod-like extensions) under a surface-induced polar field, showing that chirality is encoded in symmetry character rather than overall spectrum, and identifying essential ingredients for chiral phenomena.
AI.motivation: To understand the microscopic connection between structural chirality, electronic chirality, and chiral transport responses in artificial surface nanostructures.
AI.method: A two-dimensional cluster model with a triangular-lattice core and three rod-like extensions is analyzed under a surface-induced polar field. The electric toroidal monopole (ETM) and Edelstein effect are evaluated, with parameter-decomposition and real-space analyses performed.
AI.result: Both ETM and Edelstein effect exhibit antisymmetric and nonmonotonic dependence on structural chirality. The ETM-resolved spectrum changes significantly despite total DOS being unaffected. ETM is concentrated near vertices/rods, while Edelstein response extends into the core. Spin-orbit coupling, surface-induced parity mixing, and structural chirality are essential ingredients.
AI.conclusion: Structural chirality is encoded in the symmetry character of electronic states, and the study clarifies the microscopic mechanism linking structural chirality to electronic chirality and chiral transport in artificial surface nanostructures.

title: Symmetry-Based Design Rules for Second-Harmonic Generation in Stacked and Twisted MoS2 Bilayers
summary: Understanding how stacking controls the nonlinear optical response of two-dimensional materials is key to designing van der Waals heterostructures with tailored functionalities. Here, we establish a comprehensive symmetry-based framework mapping the structural configuration of MoS2 bilayers across four point groups (D3h, D3d, C3v, C3) to their second-order susceptibility tensor chi^(2). Using group-theory arguments benchmarked against first-principles calculations, we demonstrate how symmetry breaking controls the activation and suppression of individual tensor elements in these systems. We show that the emergence of the in-plane component chi_xxx in twisted configurations (C3 group) induces a rigid azimuthal rotation of the second-harmonic generation polar lobes, which remains frequency-independent across the entire optical spectrum, locking to half of the structural twist angle. Our findings establish a direct, wavelength-independent optical route for twist-angle determination and provide a clear roadmap for engineering nonlinear optical responses in two-dimensional materials.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a symmetry-based framework linking MoS2 bilayer stacking configurations (four point groups) to their second-order nonlinear optical susceptibility tensor, revealing that the in-plane chi_xxx component in twisted bilayers causes a frequency-independent azimuthal rotation of second-harmonic generation polar lobes locked to half the structural twist angle.
AI.motivation: To understand how stacking configurations control the nonlinear optical response of 2D materials, enabling rational design of van der Waals heterostructures with tailored functionalities.
AI.method: A symmetry-based framework using group theory to map structural configurations (D3h, D3d, C3v, C3 point groups) to chi^(2) tensor elements, benchmarked against first-principles density functional theory calculations.
AI.result: The in-plane chi_xxx component emerges only in twisted configurations (C3 group), causing rigid, frequency-independent azimuthal rotation of SHG polar lobes locked to half the structural twist angle.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a direct, wavelength-independent optical route for twist-angle determination and provides a roadmap for engineering nonlinear optical responses in 2D materials.

title: Coherence-driven origin of metamagnetism in anisotropic heavy-fermion systems
summary: A number of heavy-fermion materials exhibit magnetic field-induced metamagnetism: on applying a field along the magnetic hard axis, the magnetization first rises gradually, then jumps abruptly once a critical field is reached. Despite decades of phenomenological modeling, the microscopic origin of the pronounced magnetic anisotropy underlying this behavior has remained unresolved. The same is true of a related, long-standing puzzle: an anomalous maximum in the hard-axis susceptibility versus temperature. Both are complicated in $5f$ compounds by the dual localized-itinerant character of the relevant electrons. Here we develop an analytic $c$--$f$ theory of magnetic anisotropy in heavy-fermion metamagnets, identifying the mixed susceptibility $χ_{\rm cf}(T,h,p)$ as a single thermodynamic observable that unifies the anisotropic response across temperature, field, and pressure. We test this theory against primary and literature data for the heavy-fermion superconductor UTe$_2$, finding excellent quantitative agreement in the temperature, field, and pressure evolution of its magnetic anisotropy -- including a Kondo-coherence origin for the anomalous hard-axis susceptibility maximum, which we show is directly connected to the metamagnetic transition itself. Our results establish a general, microscopic, coherence-driven framework for anisotropic metamagnetism, applicable across the broad class of heavy-fermion compounds that display this phenomenology.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an analytic c-f theory explaining magnetic anisotropy and metamagnetism in heavy-fermion materials, identifying mixed susceptibility χ_cf(T,h,p) as the key observable. It tests the theory against UTe₂ data, showing excellent agreement and revealing a Kondo-coherence origin for the anomalous hard-axis susceptibility maximum, directly connected to the metamagnetic transition.
AI.motivation: To resolve two long-standing puzzles in heavy-fermion metamagnets: the microscopic origin of pronounced magnetic anisotropy underlying field-induced metamagnetism, and the anomalous maximum in hard-axis susceptibility versus temperature, which are complicated in 5f compounds by the dual localized-itinerant character of relevant electrons.
AI.method: Development of an analytic c-f theory of magnetic anisotropy in heavy-fermion metamagnets, identifying mixed susceptibility χ_cf(T,h,p) as a unified thermodynamic observable. The theory is tested against primary and literature data for UTe₂, examining temperature, field, and pressure evolution of magnetic anisotropy.
AI.result: Excellent quantitative agreement with UTe₂ data across temperature, field, and pressure. A Kondo-coherence origin is identified for the anomalous hard-axis susceptibility maximum, which is directly connected to the metamagnetic transition itself.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a general, microscopic, coherence-driven framework for anisotropic metamagnetism, applicable across the broad class of heavy-fermion compounds that display this phenomenology.

title: Stable valleys in the glassy landscape of a low-density parity-check (LDPC) code
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures + 22 pages, 7 figures. Comments welcome
summary: Classical low-density parity-check (cLDPC) codes defined on expander graphs are a fundamental ingredient in the construction of good quantum LDPC codes, a recent milestone in quantum error correction. They also define interesting statistical mechanics models in their own right, as they include examples of spin glass order without quenched randomness or frustration. We investigate this via a case study of a cLDPC code on a locally tree-like expander graph. Recursive techniques on trees, made possible by the locally tree-like property, probe a menagerie of stable, incongruent valleys induced by imposing different boundary conditions at low temperature. A complementary numerical study of the valleys on closed finite graphs reveals the inequivalence of the microcanonical and canonical ensemble for certain valleys.
